utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic, continued:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this chair more comfortable?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This one is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall continue where we left it off on Friday. I will remind you that we spoke about April the 18th, and about your tasks. Do you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you hear it now? Can you hear me, Mr. Tadic? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about now, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on my right ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now? Test, can you hear me now, Mr. Tadic? My assistant is telling me that she can't hear it either. Channel number 6. Can you hear me now, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Di Fazio say something or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Testing, testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So on Friday, we completed our day describing the 18th of April. You told us about your tasks that had to do with establishing and setting up the kitchen. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that you had heard that some parts of the 4th Detachment were given orders to take positions on the outskirts of the town and that certain parts of the 4th Detachment had an assignment concerning the voluntary surrender of arms. Tell us, please: In view of this assignment concerning the voluntary surrender of arms, did you have any particular tasks related to this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is something wrong with interpretation again but I'll try and respond and then we'll see. Commander, Mr. Radovan Antic, also said that while touring town and searching for people who could work in the kitchen, I should also, in case there are some issues in the 4th neighbourhood where the arms were collected, that I should see what was going on there, along those lines but nothing more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, unless I'm mistaken and looking at the transcript from Friday, the witness did not mention any voluntary surrender of arms. The portion of his evidence that I see is simply that Radovan Antic ordered the rest of the 4th Detachment to start collecting the weapons, so I don't recall anything relating to voluntary collection of weapons and it's inherent in Mr. Lukic's question, I think that we should be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Since I was reading parts of Mr. Tadic's interview I could have mixed these two things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, what did Radovan Antic tell you specifically and what kind of arms collecting was this all about? What was the role of the 4th Detachment and its members in that campaign?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the witnesses here have mentioned that the surrender of arms was a voluntary one, there was no force used, and the 4th Detachment members were not tasked with checking whether somebody possessed weapons or not. Their task was to go door-to-door and inquire whether people had weapons and if they had weapons, they would surrender it but without any use of force. So as far as the 4th Detachment is concerned, this campaign was strictly voluntary, meaning there was no force used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to use the map of Samac in order to mark some of the facilities that are important in this case. However, I can see that we do not have an ELMO here, I was told an Elmo would be brought in later and therefore I would probably like to do that later on in order to mark the sites where he moved and in order to better describe the events of that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think you can leave that part of the evidence until we get the equipment required.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we turn to a private session for a brief period of time, please? Because I would like to mention a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, on that day, did you enter the building known as the 62nd building or building number 62, did you go into any of its entrances, did you see anybody there and what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been much better if I could show it on the map but since we do not have a map, I will try to describe this and then later on we can perhaps point it out on the map. The building number 62 is in Edvard Kardelj Street. Several houses further on from my house, in the direction of Modrica. The work organisation SIT, where the cafeteria was located is across the road from building number 62. Some ten metres in the direction of my house. So if I was in the cafeteria of the SIT entity --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean the administrative building of SIT and cafeteria, are they in the same building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The administrative building is closer to my house, whereas cafeteria or restaurant is further away from my house so the restaurant is a bit further away than the administrative building and the restaurant is across the road from the building number 62. And if one stands in front of the restaurant, one can easily see what's going on across the street, and I suppose that I was standing there, and I saw some people there, and a friend of mine, Djordje Tubakovic lived in that building. He used to work in the Secretariat for National Defence for a long time and then retired from there and then I simply crossed the street --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, you said you saw people, what people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw soldiers of the 4th Detachment in the yard, perhaps seven or eight of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I crossed the street and I saw them in front of the entrance leading to Djordje Tubakovic's apartment. As far as I can remember, that building has eight entrances and I think that Djordje's entrance is the last one to the right. While I lived in Samac, that was the only entrance I ever entered in that building. So I got there and there were several soldiers standing there and I asked them what was going on and they said I -- we had heard that there are some weapons with Witness E. That was the information they had received. So I entered the entrance with them and I believe that Djordje Tubakovic lived on the first floor. As we got to his door, the soldiers and myself, there were two or three soldiers following me so as we got there, I saw a lot of footwear in front of Djordje's door. It is customary where we come from to leave shoes in front of the door before entering somebody's house. And then in the meantime, Djordje came out and I asked him, what was going on? Why is all this footwear in front of your door? And he said that all of the neighbours had come to his apartment because they believed there to be safer than in other places since he had worked in the Secretariat for National Defence. And then in the meantime, this Witness E came out, and then I asked him, "Do you have any weapons?" And he said no. And I asked Djordje whether that was right, and Djordje said, "I believe that's right." And I told the soldiers, "Guys, you've heard what the man said" and they went on. And we stood there for a few more minutes in front of Djordje's door and I said to him, Djordje, it's not a good idea for all the tenants of the building to stay in your apartment because should a shell land, there could be great trouble caused if you're all gathered in one location. So he took it as a warning of some sort. I don't know whether they followed my advice but we part -- we parted and I went on with my business.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in that building, in that entrance, did the soldiers enter apartments, the soldiers that were there, did they search the apartments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the soldiers were not ordered, nor were they authorised to enter apartments. They didn't enter the apartments because nobody told them to do it. If somebody said they had no weapons, they would simply believe them, because they were not tasked with confiscating weapons by use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally enter the apartment of Witness E?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, perhaps privacy protections ought to be exercised over that last sentence and indeed anything that might tend to identify where in the building Witness E lives or lived. Because that might be a clue as to his identity. The building is a large one with lots of apartments, I know, but if we get to anything that might tend to indicate what part of the building Mr. Tadic is talking about, then it becomes risky for Witness E.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. We can move into a private session. I wanted to avoid being in a private session for a long time but I agree. I agree. If that could lead to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will go back into private session and the redaction will be made of any identifying material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Jelena Kapetanovic, whose last name then was Stanisic? You heard her testify here. Do you know -- did you hear whether anything happened to her the way she had described it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Jelena Stanisic, I don't know her very well but I am acquainted with her. She used to work as a receptionist in a hotel many years back and she always -- and she also lives in that apartment, in that entrance. I think that she is a floor below Tubakovic, and I think that as I was going down, I saw her standing in front of her door.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you enter her apartment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the soldiers had already gone through that area and inquired about weapons. She said she had none so I saw her as I was leaving the building, as I was going down, I saw her standing in front of her door.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any armoured vehicle in front of the entrance on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no armoured vehicle there on that occasion, although later on, I heard that BOV a different kind of an armoured vehicle, had been there. It is some kind of an armoured automobile, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you or any of the soldiers standing there threaten Jelena Kapetanovic in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the soldiers saw her initially, and -- but since they didn't threaten anybody, I assume they hadn't threatened her either. At least I didn't hear any threats being issued as we were leaving the building. There was absolutely no reason for them to threaten her in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that you didn't enter any other entrances in that building, number 62. I will ask you pointedly: You have heard the testimony of Subasic Hasan. Did you enter his entrance? Were you accompanied by Zaric on that day, on the previous day, or on the following day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you about that day. Now, as to whether I had seen Zaric on the 17th, no, I didn't. On the 18th, I didn't see him. He wasn't -- wasn't around me. Perhaps he visited the building earlier but he wasn't there with me then. However, here, during this trial, I saw where Subasic lived. He lived in the part of the building facing Edvard Kardelj Street so he was able to see through his window what was going on in the yard. Even to see what was going on in Edvard Kardelj Street. So he could have seen me both in the yard in front of Djordje's apartment, as well as on the other side. He could have seen me in the street, in front of Tekstilac because his apartment is much closer to Tekstilac than is Djordje's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you never entered that entrance, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't enter any of other entrances. There was no need for them to do that because the soldiers completed the search of other entrances very quickly and it took them five to ten minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Tadic, I wonder whether you can remember what you were wearing that day when you went into number 62, Edvard Kardelj Street, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember I had a military jacket on, because it was quite cold on the 18th. I think it was even snowing a little, and this was a wind cheater and it was rather long, down to the knees. It was olive grey and it was appropriate to wear it on that day. I also had a pistol, a belt and a pistol. This was what I had to wear at that time, according to my establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And this military jacket, was it a cloth jacket or a leather jacket? What was it made of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was canvas, olive grey in colour, and it was waterproof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day or on the following days, did you ever carry an automatic rifle around?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hadn't been issued with an automatic rifle so I didn't carry one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Where is the waterworks building in relation to the cafeteria of Tekstilac? Later on we will show it on the map but could you describe it now for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wall of the kitchen was adjacent to the area of the waterworks. So that when the kitchen wall stopped, the waterworks area began. One might say that it was directly opposite building number 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: When did a tank arrive in Samac? Was there more than one tank? And when did you see a tank arriving and from what direction?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure but I think the tank arrived around the 19th of April. I didn't see it but I heard about it. My people told me that it had arrived from the direction of Crkvina. That's in the direction of Modrica so that from the direction of the waterworks, it went in the direction of my house, it passed by my house and then went on towards the embankment, the embankment of the River Sava at the mouth of the River Bosna. That's where it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 18th or the day before, although you've told us what you'd been doing the days leading up to the 18th and on the 18th, did you go to Pere Bosic Street and did you see where the Dagovic brothers lived?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know where the Dagovic brothers live. It's Pere Bosic Street on the corner of Edvard Kardelj Street, going from my house, it's the second or the third street to the right, and on that occasion, I was not in that street. I didn't go there. I may have passed down Edvard Kardelj Street but I didn't enter Pere Bosic Street on that day because there was no need for me to do that. The woman I was looking for to work in the kitchen she lived further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I was just waiting for the witness to finish his answer. If Your Honours please on Friday the witness said that on the 17th he did nothing, he stayed at home. The question by Mr. Lukic is on the 18th or the day before, did you go to this street and then the witness answers. So it's from that answer, it might -- one might take it that he's saying that on the 17th, these things happened, but on Friday, he said he stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the 17th and I'd just like that to see -- see if that position is maintained or if there is any change to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that maybe -- well, I did not want to cause any confusion. I wanted you to tell us whether on the -- well, tell us first of all whether you left your house on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice at first that you mentioned two dates, the 17th and the 18th. I thought your question referred to either one of those dates. But what I said refers to the 18th of April and this has nothing to do with the 17th. So that what I was describing that I did has nothing to do with the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have already said but I have to ask you again, because of Mr. Dagovic's testimony, you remember what he said about the tank. Did you and Zaric enter Pere Bosic Street on either on the 17th or the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what Mr. Dagovic said from this chair, and I think that it's nonsense. First of all, a tank is not a vehicle that can move through streets that are relatively narrow, and I think there is no need for a tank to go into streets such as that one, and destroy things. We know what the width of a tank is and how heavy a tank is. So to drive a tank through town in order to collect weapons, that would be really stupid, and it would also be stupid to imagine me driving a tank. First of all, at that time, I was considerably older than all the men in the 4th Detachment. They were young men. So what would I be doing with a tank at that period? So that Mr. Dagovic's stories are inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment on his testimony but only on the facts. Dagovic didn't say that you were around the tank. He said you were on the tank. Did you -- you and Zaric ever climb on to the tank?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never climbed on to a tank and I'm sure that Zaric didn't either. I don't know how I could have climbed on to the tank. I never even came near it. And looking at films and so on, I have never seen anyone on top of a tank, only behind a tank. There is only someone with his head sticking out of the turret but there is never anyone sitting on a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard Mr. Salkic's testimony, who said that you said that the barrels were to be moved away from his brother's house because you had heard that he was a good man. Do you remember ever making such a comment in those days to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Salkic's brother. I know his entire family, from Meho Paprikas to his brother and sister and his cousins. I know them all. In the building in which his brother lives, there are two flats. It used to be a family house and then Tekstilac bought it. On the ground floor, Salkic's brother lived and upstairs, my relative, Milan Vujic lived. If someone wanted to shoot at Salkic's flat, it would not be logical for them to shoot while -- because Vujic's flat was there and he was a member of the 4th Detachment. He was a company leader in the 4th Detachment and everybody knew that. And if these soldiers were around the tank, why would they shoot at that building? I wasn't there but I'm sure that had I been there, I would have said don't shoot at the house because they were able to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the 4th Detachment shooting or aiming at buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw anyone, and there was no need for anyone to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we get the ELMO, we shall go back to the map, and point to the locations that you have just described, but now I wish to ask you something about the chronology of the period we are talking about. In those days, did you have occasion to listen to the radio and were there regular broadcasts and I'm referring to that period that you are discussing in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't listen to the radio so I don't know about radio broadcasts. I don't usually listen to the radio. So I wasn't familiar with radio broadcasts. If we link up the radio with the electric power supply then broadcasts would have been intermittent because there were power shortages all the time and there was a period when there was no electricity at all. In order for a radio station to operate, it needs electricity. And how was I to guess when they would have electricity and when they wouldn't? So I didn't listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have heard quite a lot of testimony about white arm bands. What do you know about white arm bands and carrying white -- or wearing white arm bands?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard quite a lot of testimony about white arm bands, but all I can say is that members of the 4th Detachment, in the beginning, wore white arm bands as a distinguishing sign. Everybody pointed to their shoulders. There is no need for me to point now. There was pinned to their shoulders and it was a kind of badge of identification. And this didn't last long. I think that later on they even changed the colour because everybody started wearing white arm bands in order to say that they belonged to the 4th Detachment, but this lasted for a short time and then it fell into disuse. I have even heard testimony here from some witnesses to the effect that this resembled the arm bands worn by Jews in World War II. I think that this didn't even look the same, and the Jews who lived in Samac in World War II, there were about 50 of them, they probably did wear arm bands so one of the witnesses remembered that, but he doesn't remember what happened to those Jews. At the very beginning, there was a raid at Skela at the ferry, and the father of one of the witnesses operated the ferry. 100 Serbs and 16 Jews were killed. And later on, they were all -- the remaining Jews were taken to the camp in Jasenovac where they were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1941 in the park in Samac, there is a monument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic can we -- can you lead the witness to the evidence which is relevant to the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall proceed. You simply wanted to give us your position as to the testimony of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I only wanted to mention the monument in the park in Samac with all the names on it, because this was mentioned, this -- these events were mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A rally was mentioned here in front of the Buducnost building. Did you attend that rally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't, but I know that there was a rally. And those people who were not -- who did not have any assignments were invited to it but because I had things to do, there was no need for me to go to the Buducnost building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of work are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in the 4th Detachment so there was no need for me to declare whether I wanted to join the 4th Detachment or not. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether members of all three ethnic groups attended the rally? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The announcement or rather the invitation was for everybody. People passed by my house and I noticed that all my acquaintances passed by. They were all going towards the Buducnost building because they all had to pass by my house to get there. It was about 400 metres away from my house, in the direction of Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now ask that we move into private session again so that we can mention the name of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to speak about the period before the 23rd of April, which had been mentioned in an interview, and we had some evidence regarding -- relating to this date. So let us stick to this date. Had anyone invited you before that date to the Secretariat for National Defence? What happened there and what did you talk and with whom about something?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime after the 17th of April, but before the 23rd of April. I was asked to come to the Secretariat for the National Defence. That's how we used to call this institution. And there I was told that there was a possibility for me to take over the civilian protection staff. I said that I already had other commitments but they told me that there wouldn't be any problems, that somebody else was already discharging these duties, a captain. We used to call him Pile. And I had already seen him, that he had some kind of offices in Tekstilac, when I worked there, I used to see him there in Tekstilac. We knew each other and not quite well but we just said hello to each other. I spoke briefly with him and asked him what he was doing. He said I was doing something about the logistics. So that was the man Tovirac known as Pile. There was another man with me, I think his name was Dragan Pivasevic [phoen]. So they were already working there. This man Tovirac used to be in the logistics section of the TO before these events took place in Samac. Therefore, he knew what it was all about and what was necessary to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us your full name. You just mentioned his nickname but just tell us slowly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Mihajlo Tovirac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First tell us where were the offices of the Secretariat for National Defence? We shall look that into the map -- in the map?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the downtown, where the secretariat was, on a floor above a bank, across the hotel, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us generally. We shall give details later. Who did you talk to? Who asked to you come? And who told you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence was Milos Bogdanovic, and I had this conversation with him. I already said that I had known Milos for many years, that we were on rather good terms, and that he had a certain attitude towards me as to his senior and his teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did Bogdanovic tell you about your assignment? What were you supposed to do regarding the establishment of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that the civilian protection staff should be formed to operate in those newly emerged circumstances and those circumstances were rather specific, that that wouldn't be the staff as usual, it would deal with immediate tasks deriving from the circumstances that we had been currently living in. He also told me that he -- that the secretary -- the staff secretary normally appointed other members of the civilian protection staff under normal circumstances but he told me that the secretariat under those circumstances would not appoint the members but that I should choose people for that who had no military assignment. In other words, I should select some elderly people, pensioners, but if any military conscript was necessary to be on the staff, I was to ask for permission from the Secretariat for National Defence for such person to be assigned to the civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he then or later tell you where the premises would be and who should you address this issue to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that the civilian protection offices were inside the building for -- of the National Defence Secretariat, as they had always been, and there was an officer for civilian protection. I'm speaking about normal conditions. The head or the commander of the civilian protection was a volunteer who only run those actions but the officer just prepare the material and the paper and to him we referred later as the secretary of the staff. Since most probably this secretary was overcrowded, he told me that the new staff, which would have quite new tasks, can take offices in the local commune, that there were already some people working there and there was ample space there and I had no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you tell -- who did he tell you to appeal about this premises?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Volasevic the secretary of the local commune was there, and he was also the secretary of the local commune before the war, and he -- and he had the key to the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the Secretariat for National Defence, I think it's important for the testimony, was there anything in the building there that you went to frequently and what was the purpose of those offices?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of the Secretariat for National Defence, apart of what I already mentioned, there were offices for various areas, drafting officer, civilian protection officer. There was also a centre -- communications centre. That was all on the same floor, and that was under the jurisdiction of the secretary of the secretariat. That was this communications centre that had been mentioned here where I used to come later in order to get in touch with some people who reported from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 23rd of April? Who called you? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of April I went to Uniglas, where the municipal authorities were temporarily seated or relocated because the former municipality was exposed to constant gunfire from across the River Sava because the building is on the very banks on the Sava so they thought that Uniglas building will be safer, and the municipal organs were there. And I was invited to come there. There was the President of the municipal assembly, there were certain section heads, the President of the executive committee, so generally the municipal authorities worked there and that is where I went and met Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic who?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje Simic, there was also Milan Simic there but this time I didn't have any contacts with him. There was also Mirko Jovanovic and some other personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: You didn't tell us who called you to come there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Mr. Blagoje Simic, that was the first time that the two of us had a more direct contact, so to say, and he told me that Milos had suggested for me to be the chief of the civilian protection staff to which he did not have any objection. I agreed. He told me that a proper decision would be issued and that I should start establishing the civilian protection staff. I stayed there just briefly. I had a cup of coffee, and after that, I went to Volas at the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "Volas," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to Zeljko Volas, who was the secretary of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simic on that occasion or later tell you anything about the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, I received an invitation to go to the Crisis Staff, but it wasn't in the Uniglas any longer. It was relocated to the heating plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you told that based on this function of the commander of the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later Mr. Simic told me that given the fact that that was a specific function that would rather influence the civilian life in the town, that I, as the chief or the commander, would be a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us just on the 23rd of April, did you receive this decision appointing you to the commander of the civilian protection staff? We don't need to show you this document. You know what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I received it on the 23rd or 24th but of course it hadn't been ready on the date when I came but I did receive it during this period, dated the 23rd of April, although I didn't have much choice, of course, this kind of decision could not have been made in advance, because that was a kind of assignment, war assignment, for me, given to me by the secretary of -- for Defence, and there was not much choice in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you first came to the session of the Crisis Staff, had you ever heard about the Crisis Staff from whom and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the municipal assembly was not operating and it wasn't even in its building, it was all relocated to Uniglas, later I heard that that was the municipal Crisis Staff acting in lieu, temporarily, of -- instead of the municipal authorities and that the Crisis Staff was acting as civilian authorities under certain circumstances. That is more or less what I learned about the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, it's not clear from that answer whether the witness is saying that the Crisis Staff stood in for the municipal assembly that existed before the 16th or whether he's referring to some other municipal assembly, the way one reads the answer is -- it's almost as if the Crisis Staff took the place of the municipal assembly which had never operated again after the 16th. It might just -- for the sake of clarity, I think that should be made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this is more a question for cross-examination but I will ask you: Do you know when the Crisis Staff started operating, not what you heard here in the Court but just what you heard about the Crisis Staff, when it started operating?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't even know or had any information but I do now -- know now from the documents but at the time I didn't know whether the Crisis Staff was operating or was it the municipality that I thought as about municipal personnel but later when I came to the first session, I learned that there was a Crisis Staff acting instead of the civilian authorities, normally discharged by the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to the Crisis Staff but let's follow the chronology. After this meeting with Mr. Simic, what did you do after that regarding the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the local commune and there I looked for Zeljko Volas to go and see the premises. There I found one room which was vacant and he told me that we can put the protection civilian staff in that room. Then we sat together and talked a bit and I was thinking about who could be on this protection -- civilian protection staff because I didn't have any recommendations to that effect or guidelines from Milos, let alone from Simic, and thinking about that, I remembered some of my acquaintances, and I discussed this with Volas, and I took a piece of paper and wrote the names of the people I think could be on the staff. I remembered that the President of the local commune of Samac before the war was Safet Hadrialagic, aka Pop, he was the President of the local commune and I thought he was an appropriate personality and that he could be capable of doing the things that we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. Then I remembered a neighbour of mine, Trivo Lukic, who also used to be the President of the municipality. He was the manager of some companies, of a bank but he was a pensioner there, an elderly person, and I also thought that he could be useful. I also remembered another acquaintance of mine, Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter didn't get the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, could you speak more slowly? Can you repeat the first name of Mr. Popovic and please speak more slowly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His first name is Aleksandar - Aco - Popovic but I didn't mention his first name at all. Then I thought that some other guys could be there, like Ismet Ramusovic, Mate Antunovic, a retired police officer, who was a family friend of Lukic's. Zeljko Volasevic was also there. Trivo later suggested to me that we should also invite Ljubo Vukovic. So that is how more or less this staff was -- of civilian protection was established. So those were all people who had no military assignments but could have been -- could be helpful under certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Antunovic, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ismet Ramusovic, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he one of the brothers that mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the six Ramusovic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Did those people respond to your invitation? How was the staff established? How did you get together?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Zeljko because he was already versed in this kind of jobs. He knew how to get the people together, how to invite them, and he proceeded with doing that. He got those men together. We met there and agreed what to do in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you came to those premises that were assigned to you, what other agencies did you find there? Do you remember people you saw there? Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those premises, in those offices, where local commune used to be housed before, where the secretary of the local commune worked, we found Zeljko Volasevic and then later on, when Ljubo Vukovic joined in, they shared an office, or he had an office there as well. The first office next to them was vacant and that's the office that I took for myself. And the offices before those had already been taken by the Red Cross, and social work centre, I'm not sure what they were called but I saw Anka Jovanovic there, Milka Petkovic, Sveto Vasovic, Veljo and some other people who worked in that service. They had entered those premises a day or two before the civilian protection staff. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said Veljo who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velimir Maslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned these premises so perhaps could we find this out as well? Where was the telephone located in those premises, the telephone that had been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telephone used to belong to the former local commune so it had been there from before, and it was moved from one office to another office, and occasionally it would be in my office as well if I needed to make phone calls they would bring the phone into my office, and it would be there. But normally, it was in the office of the person who spent the most time there. If it was the Red Cross, then it would be in their offices. If the Red Cross people went out to do some work in the field, and didn't lock the phone before leaving, then the phone would be transferred to the offices of the local commune either in Zeljko's office or Ljubo Vukovic's office, or perhaps they would just leave an office open, unlocked so that we can access to the phone. At any rate, all of us had just that one phone at our disposal on that floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that telephone, did that operate the entire time, even when other phones were not working?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It operated continually but of course if other phones were not working then that one couldn't work either but I think that that phone had a priority or was linked to a priority telephone line and if only several phones were operational, then this phone was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when was the first time you attended a Crisis Staff session? Where was it held, what went on there and who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be a good idea to say what the Crisis Staff -- or the civilian protection staff was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us, what were the first tasks of the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Official Gazette, shown to me by Milos, it said what were the approximate tasks of the staff in peace time. Given the fact that we didn't have peace time conditions any more, the staff had a more limited kind of tasks that were important in order to organise civilian life in Samac. When we reviewed our activities, they were to be our main tasks, we concluded that we had to engage a certain number of people who would assist us with this. So therefore, in the beginning, we engaged commissioners. Since we were from different neighbourhoods, those of us who were there, and we knew the residents, we engaged commissioners from local communes or rather from neighbourhoods. Also commissioners from large buildings. So from some geographical entities, and we did it -- we tried to do it in a logical way. Those commissioners were mostly retirees, the senior citizens who were able to assist us in this. Their primary task, given that the shelling was quite intense, was to see what the situation was like with shelters that could be set up in certain parts of town. Therefore, they researched this issue to see what could be used as shelters. Since Ismet Ramusovic had a technical background, he made a list, together with another man. They drew up arrows and set up shelters, made a list of them, and then marked the shelters so that in any particular area, there was a shelter that could be used should there be a need for that. Those shelters were in residential buildings, apartment buildings, where there was a possibility to set them up, and there were also some shelters in private houses. So basically, any site that could be used was turned into a shelter. The shelters were set up in order to protect the population, and there was no force used. People were not forced to use -- to go to a shelter. Whoever wanted could go to a shelter and those who did not want to go to a shelter exposed themselves to a risk of getting killed by a shell. Naturally, people gladly used shelters whenever there was a need for that. Yesterday, as we have mentioned, my house was also one of such shelters. The commissioners also had some task relating to raising aid for refugees, finding housing for refugees. The commissioners in their areas made a list of those residents who were able to put up a certain number of refugees in their homes. So there was frequent activity of ours. People were drawing up such lists of neighbours living in the area who were willing to put up refugees in their homes. Then we collected or rather the commissioners collected blankets for the army in their neighbourhoods and so on. So those were the tasks of the commissioners of the civilian protection staff. In addition to that, we also had to set up a first aid team. Previously, the emergency aid was set up in Samac in neighbourhoods, and that was the system before, the system of all peoples defence and self defence. That was the part of our general, system. And people simply had to be reengaged in order to join the teams of people that could provide assistance to people in trouble. Before the war, that was led by Dr. Stanimirovic. Therefore he knew the people involved in this and he took this task upon himself to set up these teams in the neighbourhoods and in the buildings as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will interrupt you here because we will come back to tasks of civilian Defence but I'm interested in these initial tasks. You said that the initial tasks was to set up shelters and to find commissioners. We will -- was there anything else in those first days that you organised within the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Another important activity was to set up a team to provide emergency repairs to damages created by shelling, so we needed a plumber, an electrician and all other kinds of specialists that could do these repairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's continue chronologically, it will be easier for us to follow this. Let us go back to the Crisis Staff sessions. When were you invited and when did you arrive on the 23rd of April, when you formally became commander of civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two or perhaps three after the 23rd, I didn't remember the date, I was asked to come to the heating plant, to Toplana, so not Uniglas any more but rather to Toplana and I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time I came to Toplana. I had never been there before. I found some people there at the very entrance. There were two guys whom I didn't know. I told them why I was there. And they sent me upstairs in the Toplana building, and there, upstairs, in an office I found a large group of people sitting and the meeting had not begun yet obviously. They were having coffee, talking about general matters so the meeting had not yet been called to order. And as I've said, I found quite a number of people in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say quite a number, how many?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten, about ten, were sitting there having coffee and talking general stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some people better than others. Some people I didn't know at all. So I was introduced to some people. I greeted some people as acquaintances. There was Mr. Blagoje Simic there. I had met him before. There was Mirko Jovanovic. I didn't know him before. That was the first time I met him. Then there was Stevan Todorovic. I also had no encounters with him before. That was my first contact with him. There was Simeon Simic there and I had known him for a long time. There was Bozo Ninkovic. I also knew him from before. There was Cedo something. I knew him by sight only. Then there was somebody called Milan, I believe. Then there was Mitar Mitrovic. I had also never met him prior to that and that was the first time I saw him. I don't know if I omitted any names but those were the people that I found in that office. They asked me whether I wanted a coffee. I said yes, and then a woman there brought me a coffee. That was the first time I saw that woman too. And then after we had coffee, some people left, and one group remained, Bozo, Cedo left, and some other people, whereas the rest of us remained there. And that was then the meeting of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people, and I believe them to be members of the Crisis Staff, although I never received any official information concerning that, either concerning their appointment or concerning my appointment, I had never seen any document appointing me to that post. So before anything started, they asked me whether I had found people for the civilian protection staff, and they asked me how things were going with that. And I described it in general terms. I told them that I had done something, that we had found some people, and had done some indispensable actions, and there was visible dissatisfaction there. Mirko Jovanovic and Stevan Todorovic were particularly vociferous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. What people did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I told them about the people I had chosen for the civilian protection staff, they didn't like my choices because they believed those people to be communists. They -- all of those people had been long-term members of the Communist Party, secretaries of municipalities, secretaries of local and communes, and they didn't approve of my choice. I told them, well, I'm not among them. I don't know if that will please you. In addition to that, they simply didn't like the composition as such, but they accepted it and let it stand for the time being. The other issue they were interested in was the situation with Novi Grad, because at the time, the situation in the Odzak area was already quite complex and since I hailed from that area, they believed me to possess the best information, and I believe that that was the case indeed, I had some information, and I told them the situation was complex. I told them what had contributed to making the situation complex, and since I had information indicating that there were representatives of the international community there, I also told them that there were members of the international community there negotiating with the authorities in Odzak to have the Serbs leave the area and cross over into Samac municipality. That was the information I had, and this is what I conveyed to them. I didn't try to make it -- to sound more dramatic. I tried to use mild terms in order not to escalate tensions, because at the time, there was quite a number of people from Odzak area who had arrived in Samac. And there was a lot of concern about people in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While this is still fresh in our memory and I see that the ELMO has been brought into the courtroom, I would like to comment on the map with the witness. I have a fresh, unmarked copy of Exhibit D88/3. It's a map of Samac, and I would like the usher to put this on the ELMO so that the witness can mark the map. Mr. Tadic, you can put it on the desk but you can also put it on the ELMO and mark it there. Put it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you mark your house with number 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the technician zoom in so that we can see the map better? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark the command, or rather the administration building of the SIT company? Could you mark that with number 2?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the Tekstilac kitchen? Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was the waterworks building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks] The waterworks building was a bit away from the road, maybe some 30 metres away from the road, and the other buildings were adjacent to the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is building number 62, the residential building we talked about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the entrance that you entered, on what side is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where is the entrance where Witness Hasan Subasic lived? Could you mark that with number 7?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That entrance would be somewhere here. [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Where was the later headquarters in connection with the logistics of the 4th Detachment or rather the 5th Battalion where Mr. Tovirac worked later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the building adjacent to my building. So that would be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you mark it with number 8?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in a few more houses. Where approximately is the Dagovic family house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Pere Bosic Street and the Dagovic family lived approximately here. There was one house right next to the door -- right next to the street, and the other one was a bit away from the street, number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the old folks home building, the pensioners home?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this one here which has been shaded. It's this building here, you see, number ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says so on the map, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It says the retired persons' home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was the building of the Secretariat of National Defence and the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be here, the communications centre building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you mark that with number 11?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks] Across the street from the hotel, this is Marsala Tita Street. There was a bank on the ground floor and upstairs where the entrance was from this side here, there was the Secretariat for National Defence, in which besides the people taking care of the secretariat, there was also the civilian protection staff. It had always been there. It was there before the war, during the war and after the war. The person employed in the civilian protection was there, and the communications centre was in the same building, also upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us where the 4th neighbourhood or area, the fourth quarter was, that you mentioned, where your zone of responsibility was of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth quarter stretched from Edvard Kardelj Street towards the River Bosna. This is the River Bosna here, and this is Edvard Kardelj Street which set apart the fourth neighbourhood, the River Sava is up here and this whole area in the direction of Crkvina belonged to the fourth quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the embankment that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the embankment of the River Bosna and this is the fourth quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate where the tank was when it appeared, under number 12?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank came from this direction and it went toward the fire station. I'm not sure which of these three streets, I wasn't there, but I heard it was somewhere near the bridge. This here is the bridge leading to the River Bosna, and it was somewhere here. Whether it was next to the fire station or one of these streets, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you mark this with number 12, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could complete that task and mark it with the number 12, then I have a matter to raise concerning his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark with number 12 the location where you think the tank was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, it's more of a concern with a question asked by Mr. Lukic. My colleague, Mr. Lukic said to the witness, "Please tell us where the fourth neighbourhood or area was, that was your zone of responsibility in the 4th Detachment" and the witness went on to indicate the area. On Friday, Mr. -- the witness testified that Mr. Radovan Antic was to -- ordered that the 4th Detachment was to collect weapons not from the whole of the town but only from the neighbourhood marked as the fourth district. I understood from his evidence on Friday that the 4th Detachment was confined, the whole 4th Detachment was confined to collecting weapons from that one area of town, the fourth district, whereas now the question -- the implication in Mr. Lukic's question is that well only Mr. Tadic -- only his section, so to speak, of the 4th Detachment was operating in this fourth neighbourhood and it implies that the 4th Detachment was in fact operating in other areas of the town in addition to this specific area and it's that that I wanted to be clear about because I understood from Friday that the 4th Detachment, the whole 4th Detachment was confined to that one small area of town, and that's important to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question must have been confusing. Mr. Tadic, where was the 4th Detachment tasked with collecting weapons and where was it to take up positions in defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witnesses that will come after me will probably be able to answer this in greater detail but I can say the following to clarify this: The 4th Detachment and the fourth district have nothing in common. The districts represent a division of the town. There were four such districts. The first, second, third and fourth. The 17th Tactical Group, which in the area of Samac had certain detachments, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Detachment, that has nothing in common with the districts. The 4th Detachment covered the entire area of Samac. So the men in the 4th Detachment were not just here. It had, I think, three companies. So the first company, let's say, would be here. The 2nd company was, let's say, in this part of town. The 3rd Company, in this part of town. So that the men of the 4th Detachment were not just in the fourth district, they were all over Samac. But this is the fourth district where a part, and I've already said that, it wasn't 500 men that went there to collect weapons but only a certain number, maybe some 30 of them. So a part of the 4th Detachment went to the fourth district to collect weapons, only one part of the 4th Detachment, while the remainder had other tasks and this will be clarified later on. They went to take up positions on the River Bosna, on the edge of town, and the River Sava up here in this area, all the way to Donja Mahala. That's where Donja Mahala is that Ljubu Vukovic talked about. This is where the 4th Detachment took up positions on the edges of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has this now been clarified for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, it has, and I'm grateful to my learned friend and I'm glad that the evidence is now absolutely clear on what the 4th Detachment was doing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please draw an arrow and mark with number 13 the direction from which the men in camouflage uniform came who shot -- who fired shots in the direction of your house and from where approximately they fired shots?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is the health centre. Is that what it says here? Yes. It was in front of the health centre. They came from this direction and it was here that I saw them. It was from here that they fired shots in the direction of my house. Then they went back here and went off in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you mark this with number 13?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was then the name of this street?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Bulevar Revolucije -- revolution boulevard. That's what it says here and this street passes by my house and goes as far as the embankment on the Bosna. On the other side it goes as far as the memorial home. I don't know what its name is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, what is important here is the then location.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some other elements that are important here. [redacted] [redacted] is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would like us to move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you want me to read the numbers and say what they indicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, Miroslav Tadic's house. Number 2, the command of the 4th Detachment. Number 3, the part of Tekstilac where the kitchen was. Number 4, the waterworks compound. Number 5, residential house number 62. Number 6, the entrance to the Tubakovic flat. Number 7, the entrance to the Subasic flat. Number 8, the logistics base of the 4th Detachment, and later on of the 5th Battalion, after the 23rd of April, 1992. Number 9, the Dagovic house. Number 10, the pensioners' club. Number 11, the secretariat for National Defence and the communications centre. Number 12, the position of the tank. Number 13, the place from which the special purpose unit fired shots in the direction of the house, the Tadic house. Number 14 -- Number 15, the house of Delic and Jasarevic. I think they are not protected witnesses. And number 16, the house of Stojan Damjanovic. Perhaps we might add number 17 to show the direction from which the tank arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We may come back to this map but for now I wish to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have it marked?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D145/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, we don't have anything for number 14. It's just blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was left out in order to avoid the identification, but during the private session, the witness indicated which this number referred to so we didn't want to mark this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that was the house of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you can put aside the map. Let us go back to what we discussed before the break. You talked about your first meeting or your first visit to the seat of the Crisis Staff in the heating plant. You said who you found there. Now I'm going to ask you who were the members of the Crisis Staff. You testified to that during the interview but will you tell the Court now who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I experienced then, although I didn't receive the written decision that I was a member of the Crisis Staff, nor had I ever heard anyone receiving such kind of document, nor did I ever see the list of members of the Crisis Staff, I concluded that members of the Crisis Staff were men who were so to say regularly or very frequently present at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those that I enumerated already, do I have to repeat it again? Only the first time Savo Popovic was not present there. I probably didn't mention his name because he wasn't there at the beginning. Whether he arrived later or I don't know but afterwards, I saw him at all subsequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 57 of your interview, dated 26th of March, 1998, you mentioned these men, and I'm going to repeat that you mentioned then the names of Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, Mirko Jovanovic, Simeon Simic, Milos Bogdanovic, you also mentioned the name of Fadil Topcagic at the time. Do you know if he was a member of the Crisis Staff as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that he was appointed member of the Crisis Staff, but I never attended any meeting together with him, neither on that occasion when I came, nor on any other occasion was he at the meeting when I was there. Whether he attended any other meeting when I wasn't there, I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you mentioned that on that occasion, you saw Mr. Mitar Mitrovic, however, you didn't mention Mitar Mitrovic during the interview. So let us make it clear. Did Mitar Mitrovic have any function on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From later activities, I deduced that Mitar Mitrovic was so to say the secretary of the Crisis Staff. That means an administrative officer or maybe a recording clerk or he was the one who read out loud the decisions so these were the things that he used to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the meetings that you attended, in addition to the men that you just mentioned, were there any other people -- what was the composition of the meetings when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since at the time the Crisis Staff, in addition to the executive committee, which was sort of discharging certain powers, that was so to say the most superior civilian authority or organ, and all other segments of authority or better to say life came and presented their problems. For example, if there were any social welfare or humanitarian problems, agricultural problems, and other issues like finances, everybody -- representatives of these institutions so to say would come and present their problems. So that the sessions and the meetings of the Crisis Staff were always held in a broader circle in the attendance of people who came occasionally. Some other people would come to other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about the period before the end of April or May. How often were these meetings held and how often did you attend the Crisis Staff meetings in this initial period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this initial period, the meetings were more frequent because the problems were more complex and bigger, until the civilian authorities consolidated and the life in Samac consolidated. Later on, when things fell into place, the meetings were not so frequent. They were held only when the situation required that. Initially, it was held every other day. For example, but later, the meetings were held every three or four days or maybe once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the Crisis Staff of your own accord or were you invited to go and attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always invited by telephone or in any other manner, that the meetings was to be held at this and this time, so I used to go there when it was necessary. Maybe there were meetings that didn't require my presence were held in my absence or while I was away on a trip or had, for negotiations or if I had an interview at the communications centre at the time the meeting was held, I always gave primacy to the communications centre because I always had an opportunity to say what I had to say to the Crisis Staff on another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll discuss this further on about what you did on the Crisis Staff but we are still in the period in late April of 1992, and in connection -- and these questions refer exclusively to this period before the end of April, from the 17th of April. In that period, did you hear that any arrests were made? Who told you about these arrests and what information you had concerning this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it was really difficult for someone who was constantly in the town and with the people not to hear that there were arrests. Therefore, I learned about this in various manners, that somebody had been arrested, and in the civilian protection staff were people who told me. I also heard it from either well-intentioned or ill intentioned citizens with whom I had contacts and on occasion, I heard this from Stevan Todorovic, not officially but I did hear, and I sometimes tried to discuss with him this topic. However, he always denied that, saying that that was not my job, that I should concentrate on my duties, because that was his area of responsibility, and I agreed with that, but I did think, nevertheless, that I -- I was allowed to discuss this in a certain manner as with a colleague of mine. From my point of view, I thought for some people that they shouldn't have been detained. That was my opinion. I didn't have details but knowing some people for a long time, I was really surprised that those people got arrested. However, I always got the reply that I didn't have all information and that I should allow the informed people to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any specific names that you inquired about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember some of the names. For instance, the case of Dragan Delic. Since I knew him ever since he was a child so to say, I thought, and since in my view he was not involved in any murky business, I believed that he wasn't in this group of armed men or had some other intentions. However, he told me not to worry, that he did something else, something to do with the money, which I also didn't believe at the time. I also remember a man Zaim -- Esef Zaimbegovic. At the beginning he was a commissioner representing an enterprise but later, he was also arrested and I, as a citizen, did not believe that Esef Zaimbegovic didn't have anything to do with arming, and that he wasn't part of that group. So I also remember a surveyor, I can't remember his name now, was among those arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Todorovic inform the Crisis Staff about these arrests and the reasons for these arrests? Did you attend any such session where you heard it officially?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just in this form that I just described. If anyone asked him, he just told that there were such people but that there was not -- there was none of our business, that he was taking care about everything, and that if necessary, he would provide papers and rationale for every arrested person. Quite simply, he believed that that was his job and that is -- and he acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff -- do you know and were you present at the meeting or have you ever heard, did the Crisis Staff give any order to Todorovic concerning these arrests, in order to either arrest someone or to release someone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I hadn't been present there, I would have certainly known about that, and I'm quite sure that the Crisis Staff never said to anyone, "This person should be arrested or this person should be released." Maybe there were individual interventions, someone to be released, but I say individual, just sporadic, but there were no orders to arrest anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a member of the Crisis Staff, and the commander of the civilian protection staff and the man who was participating in the power at the time, have you ever issued an order for anyone to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and for anyone and ever. I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally endorse someone's arrest after somebody had been arrested? Did anyone ask for your approval?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't asked to give my approval, nor was I in a position to give approval because according to what my duty was, that was beyond my jurisdiction to give this kind of approvals and as a human being, I would never concede to giving such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the information that you were receiving, not only from Todorovic but possibly from other persons, did you -- were you given any more detailed reasons for these arrests, both from the official figures and both through rumours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning, and from before the 17th of April, I knew that certain groups in Samac were armed. That was no secret, that they had been secretly armed and that [as interpreted] -- therefore, the main reason for -- that Todorovic offered as a reason for the arrest was possession of arms, resistance, and things like that.
