utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said, and it was not included in the transcript, page 48, that those men were armed secretly or through TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that questionings were conducted by the police? Did you -- do you know the information acquired by the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know these details but it would be only logical that these people who were detained would be questioned. I presumed there were questionings held but I didn't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear, and if you did, when was that, for the first time, that there was beating and maltreatment of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best confirmation I received through exchanges, and I also heard from citizens, that somebody had first been maltreated and then released, so such person would tell other people that he had been maltreated and then released. However, those who were in detention, I had no contacts either with the police or with them, but later, when I had contacts with the so-called more moderate policemen, just like Simo Krunic, Savo Cancarevic, Ranko Popovic and many others, Mirko Pavic then I heard some details from them, that -- to the effect that unauthorised personnel, mostly while they were drunk, were -- maltreated the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the names of those people in camouflage uniforms were mentioned or it was unknown who did it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently, those men did it, but with them they had some locals as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Who took the decision to establish a detention -- detention units? I'm asking about the secondary and elementary schools. What information you have? Who was it to make a decision for these detention units to be formed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information available points to the police. The police were the ones who made the arrests and of course they didn't ask either me or anyone else if they thought that SUP was overcrowded they would take the TO building or if the TO building was overcrowded, they would take the school. As far as I remember, there was never discussion about this issue on the Crisis Staff or that they had any -- at any time asked for permission for this. I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose this will not going to be leading question but I guess you knew where the detention units in Samac were and where those people were held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about these detention units, not maybe from day one, but as soon as it happened, I learned about that. That was no big secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you enter those detention facilities, and if so when, and which ones, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never once entered any detention facility. Because the situation in those facilities did not suit me. A lot of my friends and acquaintances were detained there, for whom I had no explanation to offer. And I think that it was the easiest for me not to go there. If you have in mind the visit to Mato Perkovic, I do not consider that as visiting the detention facility. Is that what you're interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to that episode chronologically later on. I was just interested in hearing whether you had ever entered detention facilities and you gave your answer. Mr. Tadic, did you hear that at the end of April, I believe that the first indictment gives that date as the 26th of April, 1992, so let us uphold that date, that on that date, Dikan Brandic was killed, and if you did hear about this, who did you hear it from and what did you hear in fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this case. I didn't know that it involved Dikan Brandic. I simply heard that a man was killed. The first information I received came from Mr. Zaric, I believe, because he in a way was taken aback by that event. On that day, I took him somewhere in my car. We were looking for Nikolic, and on the way there, he told me why they were looking for Nikolic. I took him to his driver because at the time he had a driver, I believe, and he continued on with that driver, and did the things that have already been described here. So either on that day or on the following day, I learned more about the murder of this man. That man was killed in the evening, and I heard of this the following afternoon, which means the following day I learned a bit more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the following day, did you receive information that other detainees had been transferred to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that, I learned that they had been transferred to Brcko and I believed it to be a good solution for that particular period in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read out to you part of the testimony of Tihic, Sulejman Tihic, given on the 19th of September, before this Trial Chamber. Page 1441, where he describes him being present while Simo Zaric conducted a conversation. [In English] "And then Simo said he wanted to see the Lieutenant Colonel and he called for Miroslav Tadic to come, who was a sort of -- who was his assistant. Some kind of person who usually accompanied him. And then Miroslav Tadic came. They then went to Utva, I think in the car, to talk with Nikolic." [Interpretation] This is the evidence Mr. Tihic gave concerning what you just described to us. Do you remember going to the police station to get Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was no assistant of Simo's, nor his deputy. As far as I can remember, I drove Simo to the command of the 4th Detachment, not to the Uniglas company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you've said yourself, these people were transferred to Brcko and you said that you approved of it. You personally approved of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't approve of it. Nobody asked me for my approval. I was simply in accord with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant. I was interested in your personal attitude regarding that. Was Dikan's murder ever discussed at the Crisis Staff or was the transfer of detainees discussed? Did you attend any such session?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never attended any sessions where any murder was discussed, not even the murder of Dikan, whose name I learned much later. At the time, I didn't know who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to follow chronological order and will now turn to a completely different topic, but relating to this period of time. I believe we should analyse it in greater detail because it is important for the Defence's case. I'm interested in what you knew about problems with your fellow countrymen, relatives and friends from Odzak municipality. What did you know about what took place before the 8th of May incidents and so on? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the first time I attended the Crisis Staff meeting, I informed them about some of the details about events that had taken place in that area. One could say that it all started developing sometime around the 19th of April, when Rajko Djuric was killed from an ambush. His nickname was Truman. A young man, Bozic, was wounded. He was captured and transferred to Slavonia, to Croatia, to a prison there. Later on, he was exchanged, and I will mention that later. On the same day, when we heard about the incident, another team started out from Novi Grad headed by Milan Rakic, Djokin's son, because there are several people called Milan Rakic, therefore I have to indicate that his father's name was Djokin. There was another man with him and his wife, who was a nurse. They believed that there was some wounding involved and they wanted her to assist. Her name is Milena Dragojlovic. Two other young men came with them. All of them were civilians at the time, wearing civilian clothes. As they approached Prud, they were stopped by armed men. They were taken out of their car and captured. Milena, her husband and Rakic were transferred to Slavonski Brod, to Croatia, to a prison there, whereas the two young men were killed on the banks of the Sava River. I have to say that because their bodies have not yet been found or rather there is no indication of where their bodies might be, and this despite the fact that a lot of work was put in, in order to locate them. This event had a great impact on people in that area. Serbs from Dubica, as well as Serbs from Trnjak which was completely encircled, were very much afraid because of this, as were people from Lipik, and all of them fled to Novi Grad, believing that they would all be safer there if they were together. All of them were members of the Territorial Defence and the JNA, but they belonged to the 11th tactical group, which means that they were completely unrelated to our tactical group as they were on the other side of the Bosna River. So they put up some kind of resistance but it was completely hopeless because they had been completely surrounded. Shelling started, mostly from Croatia, Slavonski Samac, Slavonski Novi Grad, they found themselves in a hopeless situation and they requested the authorities in Odzak to let them leave the area, and at that time, in late April, an international team arrived. I don't know whether they were people from the European Union. I don't know. People later told me that they had little stars on their sleeves so this is why I believe them to be representatives of the European Union. They negotiated with authorities in Odzak and in Ograce [phoen] about letting them go to the Samac area. The condition was to surrender weapons after which they would be released and they accepted this condition. However, this was not implemented. Representatives of the international community left the area, having promised that they would implement this. However, this was not implemented and the time went on and the situation became increasingly difficult for these people. On one occasion, they called me from the communications centre because the operators there, who worked around the clock, had contacts between themselves before the war, they were all part of one single system. So they were in contact with each other and the guy from the communications centre told me that somebody from Odzak had called, who would like to talk to me. So the following day, I went there and he told me that the authorities in Odzak had agreed and that they had made an arrangement according to which they would let the people from Novi Grad go under the same conditions that had been arranged with the European Union and that they would let them come to the territory of our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when was this going on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early May. That was the only request they had for me. They simply wanted to inform me that they were going to cross over into Samac municipality. I couldn't say either yea or nay. I said to them, "If that's what you agreed, then that's fine."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will continue but tell us first, is this what you informed the Crisis Staff about, this story that you just told us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This hadn't happened yet when I attended the first session of the Crisis Staff. There were just negotiations going on at that time, and none of this had happened yet. All of this happened after that first session of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following meeting of the Crisis Staff, I informed them about what the people from Odzak told me about, and they had nothing either pro or contra. They were simply surprised by this and they said, we should organise accommodation for these people who were supposed to arrive on the 8 the of May, because that's what they told me, that that was the arrangement. So the civilian protection staff in cooperation with the Red Cross, with the health centre, and all of those other organs that were able to assist, organised accommodation for these people. They were supposed to happen on the separation line between Garevac and Milosevac which is some 15 kilometres from Samac. All of us went to that site. We expected that to take place in the afternoon hours because that had been the initial information so all of us went there, the first aid squads, doctors, people from the civilian protection staff, people who were able to assist in any way, the Red Cross, with their people. And a lot of other people from Novi Grad who were waiting for their closest relatives. And we stayed there waiting for them until 10.00 p.m. Nothing happened. I even went with another man to the separation line, because there was a watch guard there. There were guards there. And the guard who was a Croat told me that he knew nothing about that, that nobody informed him of anything. After that, I returned to Samac and I went to the communications centre to see if we could establish communication with them. The operator managed to establish it. However nobody responded from the other side. He tried several times but didn't succeed because nobody replied on the other side. In the meantime, a policeman came by, who was also originally from Novi Grad. So he was there out of curiosity and he told me that they had old frequencies, the ones that they used before the war to communicate, so that he was willing to use his Motorola to connect with a colleague whom he knew from before, and he managed to get the man on the other side, and he asked him about what was going on with these people, and the man on the other side said that everything was going according to the plan, and that the column was some nine kilometres long from Novi Grad to Odzak and that they wouldn't get there until noon on the following day. We parted. We all went back. And then the following day, we waited again. Again there was no radio communication, not even the man with the Motorola was not on the line. This is how two or three days went by. We were unable to establish communication, and when we didn't know what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened in fact, what did you learn later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later, I don't know whether it was two or three days, the duty operator in the communication centre, he was constantly trying to establish communication, and in the first few days, he was unsuccessful but then later on he did establish communication, and they said, those people over there, that on the following day, at about 9.00 a.m., I should be there and that somebody would be on the other side, and we could talk. So on the following day, I went to the communication centre and a man on the other side from the Odzak side was also there. I think his name was Pero. I knew him by sight. We weren't friends but I knew him and I'm sure he knew me in the same way, and he said that there had been an unfortunate incident, that the people there had been arrested, that he had nothing to do with it, and he was letting us know that they had all been arrested but he said everything was all right and the situation was under control. As he didn't know more than that, or rather he was not authorised to tell me more, that's where the matter ended and in this way, we were finally able to establish what happened to these people. One of the witnesses has already described what happened so I won't go into any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just please tell us the date when these people were detained in the Odzak municipality and not permitted to cross over into Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I now ask that this photograph be shown to the witness, which I would like to tender into evidence. Mr. Tadic, what can you tell us about this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken on the 8th of May, the day we talked about. It was taken by the Croats, who were there escorting. They used a camera but they also used a video. There was a video which we later managed to get hold of, as we did of this photograph. This is part of the column. This is my sister. And this is a man called Miljenko Topic, her brother-in-law, and they were part of the column. He probably did not have a car. In fact, I know he didn't have a car. So he put his belongings on a bicycle and my sister, her son was already detained in a camp, a group of people from Novi Grad were taken prisoner around the 28th of April, some ten days before this date. He was already in detention, and her husband didn't want to surrender and he fled to the woods, and hid there. He suspected something was wrong so he didn't want to go. He took refuge somewhere, and she set out because she wanted to see her son. And they arrived in Odzak in this column, and as the man before me said, they were taken prisoner there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you got hold of this photograph later on. We don't need any details but tell us when.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got hold of this photograph and the videotape some two or three months later because my sister had two Croatian brothers-in-law and they managed to get this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is she your sister?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D146/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on Friday, when your house and the AS cafe were discussed, we heard that a lot of people from Odzak gathered around there and this probably refers to the period we have just discussed. What were the stories going round in that period about the Serbs who had been detained at Odzak? What did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that date, the stories that went round were terrible. Even some newspapers wrote about the sufferings of the Serbs there, although they had not been able to verify their information. Some newspapers even wrote that at that time 1.500 Serbs had been killed in Odzak. I was sure in a way that this was not true and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have been through this before. What is the relevance of this to the charges against the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that we have not heard this before the Court, and I think they are relevant because of the motives of Mr. Tadic for getting involved in the exchange. I think that even the rumours of the time and the stories are important because we heard about things that did happen, about the letter to the Secretariat of National Defence and the letter sent by the Crisis Staff to various addresses, but we have not yet heard why they did so. I at least have not heard the sort of things that Mr. Tadic is talking about now, and this is important for subjective reasons because I wish to show why my client did certain things. So I think some things are relevant and should be heard before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] When you talk of the reasons why your client --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you talk of the relevance of what is to be discussed or what your client did, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to his being involved in the proceedings, the procedure related to the exchanges. All this led to his getting involved in exchanges and this is an action that the Prosecutor describes as part of persecution. So this is mentioned in the indictment, saying that persecution was carried out through exchanges. This is what the Office of the Prosecutor says. Persecution through the so-called exchanges. I wish to show not only what his personal motives were but why he wanted to work on exchanges. I do not wish to go into what others did. I only want to touch on some topics which are relevant to show why Tadic did what he did in the exchanges. I believe that he was doing something positive. The Prosecution thinks that exchanges were meant to conceal ethnic cleansing, were just a cover for ethnic cleansing but I want to show why Mr. Tadic was involved. How can the Chamber establish what his motives were and his reasons if we do not know what he heard at the time? I think it's very relevant for us to establish what he heard. Otherwise, we will only have the claims by the Prosecution that what Tadic did was meant to be ethnic cleansing. You may have noticed when we were questioning witness TW 1/3, we never asked what actually happened there. I just wanted to establish why exchanges were conducted. I am not asking Mr. Tadic as to what he knew that happened there. He's only talking about the rumours that he heard but these rumours are relevant in order to show the psychology and why something was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. You have explained that but do go through it briefly, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said briefly what you heard. Did you believe the stories that you had heard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to say that not for a single moment did I believe these rumours. I thought in human terms this could not be correct, and that these were malicious stories, and that's how it turned out to be. There were individual incidents but nothing on this large scale. I tried at all possible levels, in all my conversations, to mitigate this picture, created by malicious media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us proceed. Did you, Mr. Zaric and the third gentleman join an activity in that period in connection with the detained Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this event, the situation in Samac was very tense. Many people arrived, apart from the ones who were there from the very beginning, new people were constantly arriving and they were concerned. They brought news which were bad, which were ugly. We had to keep an eye on all this, to keep it from getting out of control, and try to create an impression of all these events. First of all, nobody knew for certain what number of people were involved, how many people were in detention over there, who these people were and so on. In this state of panic, when everybody was exerting pressure and everybody thought their own problems were the most serious and the most pressing, we concluded, and I made several attempts at the Crisis Staff to draw attention to Novi Grad, we concluded that what was most important was for us to draw up lists of people who may be detained there so that we could intervene through the ICRC or some other organisation. That's how we started drawing up these lists. I from Novi Grad, because I was already somehow in the centre of these events because people from Novi Grad were already there, Bozo Ninkovic from Dubica knew the situation concerning the people of Dubica. And Simo Zaric knew the situation in Trnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please it might be useful for you to know whom the witness is talking of when he says, "we concluded" and "we intervened" whether the witness is talking of himself, Mr. Zaric, the Crisis Staff as a collective body, or any other group, because he keeps saying "we" and it would be important for you to understand this evidence who precisely is involved in this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about this in your interview. Who was it who reached this decision? How was it decided?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a decision. We were not a formal group appointed by someone. Because we knew the situation on the ground, it was suggested by members of the Crisis Staff, someone said, "Well it might be a good idea if these three men," although we were not all there, I was the only one who was present, neither Bozo Ninkovic nor Simo Zaric were actually present on that occasion and they were not members of the Crisis Staff but they said that because we knew the situation, the three of us should gather information on the names of people who had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened with this information once you collected these names, what did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the problem of collecting names. There were over 2.000 people there between 2.000 and 3.000 so it wasn't a simple task. Especially not in the case of Novi Grad, which had the largest number of people, and of course I didn't know them all, so the people who were there and who were more familiar with the situation, we all entered names into the list. Bozo entered the names that he knew and that he heard from other people in relation to Dubica, and Simo did the same in relation to Trnjak. A same -- a group of the same sort was established in Belgrade, where people also organised themselves into an association gathering information that was known in Belgrade. Family members would report the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the interview, Mr. Tadic, what did you do with these lists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these lists were handed over to the International Red Cross in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any role in connection with appeals made to the general public?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these appeals -- these lists were a kind of appeal, but I have to say that although this is also in the interview, a far larger number of people, of names, reached the International Red Cross than was actually realistic, because many names turned up again and again in different lists, and they didn't know this so that in Belgrade, the number of people reported to the ICRC amounted to about 4.000. And this cry for help was then raised to a higher level. Letters were written and sent to all sides asking for help. In Belgrade, an association was established of detainees from the area and they sent appeals for help to certain addresses. I remember they wrote to a congresswoman in America, her name was Bentley and then to the world organisation of Serbs in Geneva, and in the end I went to see the patriarch but that was later. So that everyone people thought might help was an addressee. They thought that someone might be able to help. So they wrote letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the 8th of May, was there any mention on the Crisis Staff about the situation and how frequently? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this situation took place and I mentioned that we discussed Novi Grad earlier but after these developments, always at the Crisis Staff meetings, the item number 1 on the agenda was the situation in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who informed the Crisis Staff on that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly I provided information relating to Novi Grad. We often concluded the sessions with this item, as soon as that problem was resolved the sessions were concluded and after I made my presentation, I would leave the session and go elsewhere to do other jobs. So that was the situation which was very important and crucial and could not have been avoided at any level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the houses of those people, of the houses of your family, at the time when they were detention? When did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the houses -- after the 8th of May, the houses were mainly set on fire. Most of them were burned. I could even say about Dubica, the village that used to have 210 houses that in mid-July, 1992, there were no more than a dozen or to be more precise, 18 houses that were left intact that were not burned which means that 102 [as interpreted] houses had been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you find out that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out about that after the first exchange, about one part, and that was done officially, but with every subsequent exchange we received more information. But the major part of information arrived after -- the major when the 1st Krajina Corps took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the time for a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Presiding Judge are we going to have our next break at quarter to 2 just so I can plan my topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are supposed to have our next break at 13.30 and then continue in the afternoon from 1500 hours to 1630 that was the new schedule for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday only and then on Thursday, we revert to the mornings only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I would like now document with internal marking PDB2/3, to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can you tell us briefly about this document? Do you know who drafted it and what it pertains to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the title, it is clear which organ drafted it, Ministry of the Interior, municipal secretariat for internal affairs, Odzak municipality. I would just like to say that next to the numbers 3/0203, there is a date, 11th of April, and the date is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a typing error, because the events described took place in May, and this can be clearly seen in the fourth line of the explanation where it says that on the 11th of May, 1992, from 1500 until 1800 hours, they toured the area of Donja Dubica and Novi Grad. So it means that the date in the upper corner was a typo, because in April, around the 11th of April, there were no hostilities and there couldn't have been a situation described in the text of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The names that are mentioned here, whose houses are these? What is the ethnicity of the owners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can conclude that based on the last names, that these are the houses of the Serbs from Donja Dubica and Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give us a yes or no answer. Do you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know most of the people from this list. Under number 3, the name is Jefto Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have to go into names. We don't have to spend so much time on this document but if you think it's important go ahead and say it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's important. Jefto Kovacevic is the father of my brother-in-law and my brother-in-law was the President of the municipality in Odzak. Fortunately, on the 8th of May, he was not in Odzak. He had left earlier. And he was held to be responsible. Under number 24, is the name of Djuric Rajko, called Truman. Under number 26 is the name of Sreto Minic who will be mentioned later. I don't want to keep you any longer and I'm sorry that this document was not placed on the ELMO. I didn't need it in front of me to mention the names. And the rest of the people in the courtroom didn't see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Everybody will get the opportunity to see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be given a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D147/3. And ter for the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction for the record. Before the break, you mentioned on page 65, the number of the houses destroyed in Dubica, and written here there was 102, whereas you mentioned a different figure.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the figure of 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could now the witness be shown two photographs, please, together? Can you tell us what is depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph shows the house of my daughter in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was this picture taken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my daughter on the stairs here. This photograph was taken before the 17th of April, 1992. As I've said, my daughter lives in Switzerland and she only comes to the area occasionally, or she used to come occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next photograph, please? What can we see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph shows the same house, and nowadays, this house doesn't even have this front facade because the time has taken its toll.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please be given numbers for these two photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph showing the house will be D148/3. The photograph showing the burned house will be 149/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have two more photographs but I will give them one by one so that the identification goes more smoothly, and then we will complete with the photographs. What can we see on this photograph, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the house of my wife and me the way it looked about a year ago, and it is in a worse shape today. This is just a view from one angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is this house located?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be given a number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D150/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last photograph, Mr. Tadic, for the present time, what is shown here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the house of my brother, also located in Novi Grad. He's been living in Germany for more than 30 years and when the house was set on fire, he wasn't there. The house looks the same nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we be given the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D151/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, please tell me when the information reached Samac about what was going on in Odzak municipality, was there any desire to -- for revenge in Samac municipality? Was there any desire among the population to avenge for these events? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fully informed about this, and there was no such thing taking place. Nobody's house was destroyed on purpose, nor set on fire, but some houses were damaged by shelling and there were no other instances of revenge-taking. I regret that we did not see the picture of my sister's house because it is in a very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do have that photograph ready. Perhaps we can tender it in later on. No, let's put another photograph before the witness. Is that the picture?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is self explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this is the house of the sister whose photo we have seen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we get a number for this photograph as well, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D152/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, at that time, when you learned about what had happened to your property and the property of your family, relatives, did you have any desire to avenge with respect to your Croat neighbours or friends?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then and not now [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You in fact said not then and never?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will return to events in Odzak later on when we get there chronologically but I'm interested in another issue that has been discussed here before this Trial Chamber, relating to the crime in Crkvina. In the interview conducted with you, the OTP mentions the date of the 7th of May, 1992, and I can see that date mentioned in some other indictments before this Tribunal. So we will abide by this date. Do you know something about this event? If so, what? And whom did you learn it from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of the event that took place and clearly that was an atrocious matter. There were whispers about it around town. There was -- the rumours were whispered around town regarding that. However, I never heard anybody say anything publicly regarding that. I talked to Mr. Zaric regarding this. And I think that it was from him that I heard for the first time about that terrible event. But there was also tete-a-tete.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you learn some other information from Zaric regarding the event and his activities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later found out from Zaric that he had been in Belgrade. He went there because of this event. However in Belgrade, they were shocked and unwilling to comment on this. And they didn't do much about it. That's what I learned later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to the other people, the remaining people from that warehouse? Did you learn anything regarding that and is there an event you would like to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been mentioned here that the residents of Crkvina intervened fiercely and asked the police to remove those people from their village because they did not agree with what had happened there. So the remaining people were returned to Samac. Now, as to where they were returned, I know nothing about that. First of all, I never knew what people were in Crkvina. A number of 52 was mentioned here. I never learned the identity of the people who were in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. You mean people who were imprisoned, detained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire group of 52. I never learned of the final list of people who had been killed in Crkvina. What was mentioned were where those people were from but I was never able to get to the exact, final number, the numbers of 15 or 16 are mentioned, sometimes even 17. Not even in the police was I able to get that list. They either didn't have the list or they wouldn't show it to me. The people who were transferred to Samac, they were eye witnesses to that event and they all gave different accounts of the event. There was an eyewitness from the other side, and he also gave a statement which differs from others quite significantly. What I learned about that was as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. The Prosecutor wanted to clarify something, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I did, as a matter of fact. If Your Honours please, for this evidence to be of use to you, you should know, I submit, when Mr. Tadic contacted the police to try and get the list of murder victims, and who he dealt with when he was informed that they didn't have the list or that they wouldn't show it to you. Otherwise, the evidence is largely meaningless. He might have done it last week or he might have done it in May of 1992. The people he dealt with is also important. So for you to be able to use that information, you've got to know what he did with some more specificity, I submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this will become clear once the witness fully describes this. Did you, and if so, why, ask for these lists in the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police kept records or made lists based on the location, so people who were in the TO and the people who were in the elementary school and the secondary school, the lists were maintained. However, there was never ever a list of people who were kept in Crkvina or the people that remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first exchange, which took place on the 25th or 26th of May, 1992, Lugar came.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Came where?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Came to see me at the civilian protection staff, and arrogantly said there was an exchange yesterday. I said yes, and then he said did anybody from Crkvina leave? And I immediately said no. Without actually knowing whether somebody had left or not, I just thought that that would satisfy him, and he said, "Well that was well done," meaning that I had something to do with it. I was in charge of it [as interpreted]. Make sure that nobody leaves Crkvina in the following exchanges. I said fine, they won't. Although I had no intention of actually following what I said. I didn't know what people were supposed to leave. I didn't know whether in fact they would leave. So those were empty promises. I just said that to placate him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction. The witness said, "I was not in charge of it".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, after that, when you were involved in exchanges, did you have anything to do -- did you have any activities regarding finding the bodies of those who were killed in Crkvina? Please tell the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will speak on my behalf, and I will say that neither I, from Samac, nor those from the opposite side, had any detailed information regarding Crkvina. The first information received by them, and very superficial information at that, came after the first exchange because later on, it turned out that none of those people who were in Crkvina went in that first exchange, because they were in the secondary school and then later it turned out that they were not in the secondary school but at another site so none of them were exchanged then. It was simply said that they had heard that something had happened in Crkvina. So they were given a -- non-reliable information regarding that. And in the following discussions that we had, which were quite intense, Crkvina was never mentioned as a specific location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say in our discussions, what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contacts between the Serbian and the Croatian side, if Veljo and I went and other members of the commission, and negotiated with people from the Croatian side, we never touched upon the case of Crkvina itself. We simply mentioned individual names. We said that individual persons had been sought, and it was discovered that some of those individuals had perished in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Despite the fact that there was no specific search for the bodies, did you undertake anything to find them and if you did, why did you do it and how did you do it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the commissions that operated were tasked with collecting all possible information relating to the missing persons. That was both the task vis-a-vis the International Red Cross was also involved in collecting data and also vis-a-vis the opposite side from which you also expected reciprocal data concerning missing persons. So that was part of our regular activities in collecting these data. When we learned more later about the whole affair, I tried to follow certain traces that could possibly lead to a desired goal. However, it was very, very, very difficult to get in touch with people who knew something, especially since everybody was afraid of the situation surrounding this event and this case that in a certain manner at that time aroused fear in people. Nevertheless, I managed to gather together some 40 or 50 people and I talked to them and I found a certain lead and I asked those people to help me in finding these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the same problem is arising again. What commissions were tasked with collecting all possible information relating to the missing persons? Furthermore, is that a reference to missing persons in Crkvina? Furthermore, when was this done? And furthermore, if Mr. Tadic managed to gather 40 or 50 people and talk to them and conduct some sort of investigation, when was that done? The evidence is really not going to be of any benefit to you unless you know those sorts of details. Now I know that I can take these issues up in cross-examination but it's beneficial for the Trial Chamber and for Mr. Tadic to -- for his position to be made absolutely clear. Furthermore, it's not a matter that I wish to spend time on in cross-examination, clarifying his story so that we know exactly what he's saying because that eats into and detracts from the amount of time that I have available for cross-examination. So I do suggest that we should be clear about those sorts of details when he's giving evidence like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will clarify this issue, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you mentioned that all commissions were involved in searching for missing people. Which commissions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowadays, and then, all the commissions in the territory of the former Yugoslavia were entrusted with this task. That means, if I have to enumerate them one by one, those were all the commissions that existed in the former Yugoslavia, including the one in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the exchange commissions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the exchange commissions are still at this very moment doing excavation work and collecting data and this work is still in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know how these commissions are called? What is this commission of Republika Srpska called?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission for searching for missing people. That is more or less the name. I'm not 100 per cent sure. There is such commission in the Serbian part, in the Muslim part, in the Croatian part. It exists in Croatia, in Yugoslavia, and these commissions are still working up to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be fully clear, do you know that the same people are working on these commissions now that used to be involved in the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are still people on these commissions who had been involved in this when I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you conducted these interviews with some 30 or 40 people, when did that take place and what ensued?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started these interviews, let's say as soon as the conditions were favourable, and that is after Lugar had left the area. In other words, these interviews took place, I think, towards the end of 1992, when he left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In those activities of yours, did you have an opportunity to bring a large number of forensic experts and pathologists in order to unfind -- undiscover this location at the level of the republic or the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I wanted to say. Once a location has been identified with the aid of witnesses who had some kind of knowledge, then expert teams would come to do the job. I asked the commission of Republika Srpska to come from Banja Luka, having told them that I got certain information and they made efforts to search the area that was marked or identified. Unfortunately, despite the whole day of work, they failed to find anything. I must add something. I have been listening very carefully to the evidence given by Mr. Todorovic, and he mentioned this problem. He even mentioned that he had made a sketch that he delivered to the Prosecutor. I wanted to see that sketch in order to make a comparison with what I knew, in order to find a certain solution. Of course, I did not get this sketch up to this date, so I was unable to make comparison and see if there are any discrepancies with what information I had. I even heard that Mr. Todorovic went on the ground to show this site where these people were. So it would be advisable if he had any information to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, what were your motives and why were you so eager to find the bodies of those people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot say that my motives were of a professional nature as a member of the commission. Although other members of other commissions and with this I refer to all the commissions, were mainly motivated by professional reasons. In my case, in spite of that motive, there was another one, because a large number of Serbs were also missing, and I thought that others would help find them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On Friday, you mentioned Luka [Realtime transcript read in error "Lugar"] Gregurevic, who frequented the AS cafe and this Chamber knows very well that he was one of the men --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Luka Gregurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Lugar Gregurevic, it is the same mistake that was made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are talking about Luka Gregurevic, who I knew well. Then there was Ivo Tuzlak and he was also mentioned. I also knew him well. He worked together with my wife for 20 years. Then there was Josip Orsolic. He had a store in the house of my neighbours. His name was Resakovic and we had coffee on a daily basis, either in the restaurant or I went to his store whenever I needed something. So we lived next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we will take a break now and I want to ask you, are you capable of continuing this evidence in the afternoon because I see that you are rather upset and excited.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since nothing is up to me...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you capable health-wise to endure this in the afternoon? I think the Chamber would like to know that because we would like to have your testimony be focused and of good quality because that is in the interests of this Chamber and in my interests as your Defence counsel. I see that on a few occasions, you got very excited. So in view of your health condition, do you think you will be able to continue this afternoon? We need to tell this to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have put everything -- I put this process above everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break and continue at 1500 hours up to 1630. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall go back to a topic that precedes chronologically what we have been talking about. Can you hear me well, Mr. Tadic? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all right. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your contacts and that you went to the communication centre when discussing the events of the 8th of May. Before these events, did you have any contacts with the Odzak municipality through the communication centre? And how did it come about that you turned up in the communication centre so we are probably going back in time. Can you tell us when your contacts through the communication centre began?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I have already explained this. I said that I had the first contacts after the 23rd of April, and that I learned through these contacts that the international community was there and that these negotiations were going on there, and that was on one or two occasions before the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the episode you mentioned in your interview concerning the exchanges of Sreto Minic and Milan Stanisic and when these events took place, who did you contact on the other side and who did you talk about in connection with these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both these events took place in late April, 1992. I think that first Milan Stanisic was exchanged in the circumstances in Novi Grad, he was seriously wounded. I think he was wounded by a shell, and in one of these talks, the people on the other side told me that his condition was extremely serious and that since they are unable to treat him in the hospital in Odzak, it would be a good idea for them to hand him over to our side so that we can take measures to have him treated. I agreed with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 80, line 1, you said Milan Stanisic was surrounded in Novi Grad and that he was seriously wounded. You didn't mention the name exchange -- you didn't mention the exchange then.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. This Milan Stanisic was seriously wounded and I accepted their suggestion that we should take him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who you talked to on the other side in these talks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I think it was either Stjepan Mikic or Pero Zecevic, one of the two was there at the talks then but I'm not sure which of these two was there. One of them was. So I accepted this proposal, but they asked that a man called Ilija Barukcic go over to their side. He hailed from Prud, and there were no problems provided the man wanted to go. He went to this man. The representative of the Red Cross, Veselin Ivkovic, and he talked to him and after a certain time, they came to my house. We sat in the garden. It was a nice day. And I told him who this was about, and he remembered that this young man was a son of one of his friends, because he was married to a Serb lady from Donja Dubica, so this man Barukcic was married to a Serb lady and this was a son of a friend of his, and he said, "I will go" and someone said no problem, just come back when you want to. And then he got into the car with this Ivkovic and we went to this place that had been agreed upon at the Garevac-Milosevac demarcation line and an ambulance went with us. Dr. Hecimovic was there and a nurse. There was a nurse, but I can't recall her name at the moment. And there was a representative of the Red Cross, and when we arrived there, they brought this Stanisic on a stretcher and the man from the Red Cross took him and brought him over, and put him in the ambulance. His condition was extremely serious. I looked in through the front door, I didn't know him but I said, "Young man, how are you?" And he could barely speak and he said all right. So I asked the doctor what he thought of his condition and the doctor says -- said, if he managed to reach the hospital his life might be saved. The nurse was called Navenka and he told Navenka that that they were going to Pelagicevo right away and then from Pelagicevo he went on to Belgrade and he did survive but he's an invalid today in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This man Sreto Minic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "certificateeto"] Sreto Minic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this in the same period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was in early May, I think. I think it was in the beginning of May. He was an elderly man. Maybe 15 years older than me, and he was ill. He was in the hospital in Odzak. There was a doctor from Samac, her last name was Hecimovic, who was working there, and through the radio connection, she asked or rather she said that she wanted to release this Sreto Minic from hospital and have him cross over to our side, and in exchange she asked that her brother, Aziz Hecimovic, also known as Ciger go over to their side. I knew him. He was a former pupil of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 125/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I don't know what your transcript shows but line 17 in page 81 is not very clear to me. As is line 18. Some -- some -- odd words "certificateeto" I just wonder what the question was because I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To assist my colleague, I apologise, it was mispronounced the name of a certain person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was about Sreto Minic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only Minic and this other word is instead of Sreto.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document on the ELMO? Does this refer to what you have just been talking about? And the date mentioned, the 2nd of May, on the document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was Sreto Minic who brought this document along with him when he came. I asked the people from the Red Cross to go and find Aziz. Aziz came and I told him that his sister was looking for him. That she wanted him to go. He wasn't very willing but he said, all right, I'll go and see my sister and then I'll come back here. If you want me to. And then he went to his sister's in Odzak but he didn't come back soon. Later on, his wife and two children went to stay with him in Odzak. He asked for his wife and children to go to him. So his wife and children went to be with him in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One small correction, in the transcript it's on page 82, line 20. Maybe it was some misunderstanding. The witness didn't say if you want me to. Well, meaning that he wanted the witness to go on the other side. The -- what the witness actually said was that when he asked, do you want. He said all right, maybe, I don't know, I'm not very happy about it, and then he asked him all right, I will do it, something like that. It was not the witness who decided instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, to avoid misunderstandings in the transcript, do you remember what this man Aziz Hecimovic said when you told him that his sister on the other side was looking for him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he wasn't very happy to be sought but that he would do as his sister wished and go to their side or rather to the side of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Why were you going to the communication centre? Was the other side asking for you to come there? Did you know the people on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew these people who were talking to me, and they knew me. I knew Stjepan Mikic especially well, who was a colleague of mine. He had worked in the school in Odzak. And we saw each other very often. He lived close to my brother-in-law. So I often went to have coffee with him, if I went to see my brother-in-law and he wasn't at home. And we also knew each other from school. We'd known each other for a long time. And I knew this man Pero, Pero Zecevic, I knew him well too and he knew me even better. And some other people, Ante Simic, Stjepan Ivankovic, the one who signed this. I knew them well too and they knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be shown document P71?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you know whether a decision was issued at the Crisis Staff on the arrest and isolation of members of the Croatian ethnic group and their placing in important facilities in the town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never attended a session of this nature, nor did I ever hear that a decision was adopted on isolating anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your work in the Crisis Staff, did you ever see this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never seen a document like this or anything similar to it. Of a similar content.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Crisis Staff, in the period mentioned in this document, or at any other time, was there ever discussion of any citizen of any ethnic group be put in a vital facility or isolated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No discussion was ever held on this, nor did this ever happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have finished with this document. In your interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Tadic, just one question with respect to your last couple of answers, concerning this document. You said that no discussion was ever held on this, nor did it ever -- nor did this ever happen. Do you mean while you were there? Or do you mean that you know it was never discussed even at meetings of the Crisis Staff that you were not present at? It might be helpful if you could address that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that this was never discussed, I meant of course in my presence. When I was not present, I didn't know what was being discussed, but I also wanted to say that such a measure was never implemented. No one was ever put on a facility as a shield. I would have known about it. I would probably have heard of it, if nothing else. So that's why it's my opinion that this was never discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, just arising both from the line of my -- questioning by Mr. Lukic and also arising from Your Honour's question just asked, is -- I wonder -- and for the sake of clarity, I wonder if the witness is saying that, A, no Croats were ever taken to vital facilities, and B, never isolated, that they could be two separate things and I just wonder if the position of Mr. Tadic is that neither of those two things were ever discussed or resolutions passed implementing such actions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about this, I was speaking of taking people to vital facilities, and I asserted that no one had ever been taken to a vital facility and while I was in the Crisis Staff I never heard any talk of this. But I was not speaking about isolation. I didn't say anything about isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Crisis Staff, was there ever discussion of isolation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no discussion of isolation either, but it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about this in your interview, and the Prosecutor asked witnesses questions about your statement of the 26th of March. In the second half of May, were there any detentions and what do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- this is not a specific enough question. Can you please remind me of what is contained in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My specific answer [as interpreted] was whether in the second half of May, 1992, Croats were arrested and detained from the surrounding villages and on what grounds it happened? Is it clear -- more clear now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. In those days, I knew nothing about that, but later, I heard that a number of Croats from the area of Asici, Donji Asici were arrested including the villages of Novo Selo and Hrvatska Tisina. I believe that was the area. And that took place after the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, Mr. Tadic, but I just wonder when you say in those days, I knew nothing about it, but later you heard, how much later did you hear about these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A couple of days later, I heard that they had been arrested, but an event that took place before that, I knew about it immediately in fact. I think that that was on either 14th or 15th of May. I cannot say specifically. A group of soldiers of the then 4th Detachment, the majority of whom were from Novi Grad, and there were some neighbours of mine as well, my next door neighbours, they went to change shift in Grebnice and they took exactly this road that runs through the Srpska Tisina and Hrvatska Tisina via Novo Selo towards Grebnice, and that is where an ambush took place and it had been mentioned before, and when fire was opened at this bus, where some 30 soldiers were on board, plus the driver of the bus, I think that was a master bus, that's the name of the maker, or the company, the driver sustained 16 penetration wounds and a number of soldiers, some ten of them, were either lightly or severely wounded, but thanks to the circumstances that the driver, being wounded, collapsed, and held the driving wheel, and he also pressed the gas pedal with his foot, he simply just went out and brought the bus some 150 metres away up to the line where it was safe. And due to that, no more severe consequences occurred. Only people got wounded. And the soldiers survived. Of course with the consequences that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there many severely wounded people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some dozens wounded soldiers, plus the driver, three or four of them were from Novi Grad. Later on, they were hospitalised in Bijeljina and they all survived, I think one of them remained an invalid in the leg. His name was Rakic from Novi Grad. Also the driver is an invalid and a Croat called Kalinic sustained a wound in the throat. The rest sustained light injuries and they survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours -- I was going to invite the Trial Chamber to press for an answer to Your Honour's question, which I submit has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because I was wondering about these details and the relevance of them to the charges against the accused. Because we are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In fact, on the same note as both our Presiding Judge and Mr. Di Fazio, my question related to the incident already referred to, but Mr. Tadic, you then elaborated on some other event which had happened before, which really didn't relate to what we were already discussing. So it's a little bit confusing, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I wasn't able to take the floor, but it is quite obvious from Mr. Tadic's interview that he sees the relation between the two incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, tell us where did this incident happen in the territory under whose control and how was it related to the events that we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my understanding, what I just described was a cause and what we just mentioned earlier was a consequence. I wouldn't like to tell some details and pretend to be an expert, but the background, in the background of this army that was positioned on the line, this undesirable incident took place and to my modest, humble judgement, the army couldn't permit to have a fifth column in its rear, and that is -- that is what resulted in the arrests of those people, in order to avoid these kinds of incidents because on a daily basis, soldiers travelled down this road to the line, not only down this road but other roads as well, and if those incidents were allowed to happen, it would have been dangerous for the army. And at the time, nobody knew who set up this ambush at the time for the soldiers. Only later was it discovered how the ambush was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that at the time revealed -- first of all, is it the area with Croat populated villages of the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the Croatian area, Donji Hasici, Hrvatska Tisina and Novo Selo villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that people in those villages were armed? Were there any rumours relating to the villagers there? We heard that in previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an insight into this situation but I knew that they were armed and that some of them surrendered their weapons and that is what I also heard here, because at the time I didn't know any details about confiscating of arms, detentions and things like that, but later on, I got the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these people from these villages were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were detained at the education centre, it is sometimes called secondary school but that's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the same period, some other people were taken to the cultural club in Crkvina? Did you hear anything about that? Do you know what was the background of that event?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason and the cause was but I know that it did happen because some people who were very close to me helped with providing shelter and food for those people in Crkvina. I know that the Red Cross took food there and a driver, Ismet Kurtic, who worked for the civilian protection staff, drove food stuff every day to those people, whatever else was necessary. Otherwise, I don't know why they were taken there, but according to Ismet's stories and other people from the Red Cross, it lasted for a couple of days and then they were returned to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us move to another subject, the shelling of Samac. We heard a lot about this in this Court but I would like to establish a connection between this and what you did, but first of all, we would like to hear -- to see a videotape that we have prepared, but before, allow me to explain to the Chamber that this is some 15 minutes footage showing demolished buildings in Samac. I made an excerpt lasting some three minutes because it will take too long to look at every building, but this footage is part of the video cassette that we have already tendered as evidence. The video was shot in 1998. So can we please see this three-minute video and Mr. Tadic, you can comment on it. This is Exhibit D103/3. Could you please play the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can recognise this facility, can you tell us? It's a paint shop but if you can't see it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to discern here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could please the technicians press forward so maybe later you can recognise it. Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one neighbourhood in Samac. The quality of the video is not so good. This building was the one already mentioned. I think that one of the witnesses mentioned this building. This is the place where the shell hit it. This is the building with 18 flats and Sveto Vasovic and an unnamed witness also lived nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please stop the film here? Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is very near my house, maybe some 50, 60 metres away. It belongs to my neighbour, Bozica, which was -- who was also mentioned before. It was hit by a shell, and this lady neighbour of mine was Bozica, was severely wounded, and very close nearby, maybe some 5 metres away --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you're going to see it. Can you tell us what do you see next to this building? What is this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We have to go, we have to rewind the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, if you could stop here.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it couldn't be better than this, I'll try. On the right-hand side, this white part of the building is health centre. It has been mentioned many times here. Two shells hit this house and one of them fell very close to the health centre. You can see from the footage how these two buildings are close to one another. So this health centre has been renovated, thanks to a donation from an international organisation in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We can continue now, please. [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, what is this? We don't have to stop the video. Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the corner of the streets of Edvard Kardelj and Bulevar Revolucije, you can see my house here, also the Mladnost restaurant. This is the entrance to my building, and if you can freeze here, you can see exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the bullet holes from bullets fired at my house on the morning of the 17th of April. This is just one little part. There are holes all over the whole glass plate here. These are all the bullet traces on my house that was hit from firearms on the 17th of April, 1992, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are these traces still present on your house nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
