utterances.text: Yes. In some places. The glass bricks or the wall made of glass bricks has been repaired but there are traces in other areas and there are still bullet holes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we saw practically in every testimony before this Chamber that shellings were frequent. I would like to ask you something that I'm interested in but has not been covered extensively by testimony so far. What was the situation like concerning shellings of villages in Samac municipalities? Once we see this movie, it will become clear to the Chamber what exactly was going on then but please tell us what was the situation like in villages?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was similar to the situation in Samac. The villages were also heavily shelled. And one can see that from the list of the civilians who were killed. There were civilians killed in practically every village, women, children and the elderly, every village except for Zasavica. So all of the villages in Samac municipality were shelled except for Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get back to Zasavica later on. Now, regarding the shelling, in early May, 1992, were the shellings particularly frequent and what happened during that period of time, in which the civilian protection staff was especially active? You've mentioned shelters. Now, let's turn to this other activity of the civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to emphasise a particular period of time and say that shelling was especially heavy during that time. Shelling was continuous and always intense but in the beginning it hits you the hardest. Maybe even a few shells would hit you hard until you get used to that. So people remembered the month of May particularly well because they could tell that it was no joke and it could lead to a serious situation. Following that, an evacuation of the population was organised. People left for Serbia. This has been explained in detail here. I would just like to say that the civilian protection staff attempted to provide vehicles which would transport the people who had applied to the Red Cross, the elderly, women and children, to the holding centre in Serbia. I think it was called Krnjaca or something like that. I would just like to add that some 150 women, children and the elderly left Samac but also from other villages, Crkvina, Obudovac, Batkusa, in these villages, transports were organised for the residents as well. So in that first convoy, some 300 to -- 350 to 400 people left Samac municipality. All of them were housed in the agricultural compound in Krnjaca. I went to visit those people there and I saw where they were housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us where Krnjaca is? We omitted to say that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in Serbia. In the vicinity of Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't put the document before you now but do you remember whether families of members of all ethnicities living in Samac were able to go and be evacuated if they wanted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can tell so from the list. Everybody who felt the need to leave was able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following that evacuation, were there any other people interested in organising a similar campaign and was something done regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people found decent accommodation. It was pretty decent accommodation and the food was good too so that the rumour spread out through Samac. After that, there was a large number of people who wanted to leave too. However, the holding centre, the reception centre, was already full. It couldn't take any more people. Through the Red Cross of Yugoslavia, or rather of Serbia, we managed to find -- we didn't manage -- we found another centre but we were unable to organise another evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown photograph D36/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Other witnesses have commented on this photograph but I know that you have the comments you wanted to share with us as well. What was the role of the Red Cross concerning glazing and funerals, so all of the tasks of civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you mean the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the civilian protection. We will take a look at the photograph first and then we will turn to the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the building called the pensioners' club or the pensioners' centre. It's been shown here a number of times. This street here is Pere Bozic's Street and this street on the opposite side is Djure Djakovica Street. You can see there are apartments upstairs, whereas this area here, before April 17th, those were premises of the local commune and then below here is where the pensioners' club was located. This was a coffee bar where pensioners gathered. In this part here, there is a separate entrance leading to several offices, and those were offices of pensioners, hunting club, and I don't know who else had offices there, whereas the entrance into the pensioners' centre is from Djure Djakovica Street, so one had to go first into the courtyard and then enter this office here from the courtyard. On the 17th, or rather after the 17th of April, those who had been mentioned here were housed here, as was the headquarters of the civilian protection staff. This last window here was the window of the secretary of the local commune's office, and this office next to it was the civilian protection staff office. To get to the offices upstairs, as well as to these apartments up here, one had to go from this part here so the entrance was a common entrance, both for offices and for the apartments. So once you got to the first floor, there was a hallway leading here and then staircase going upstairs to where the apartments were. This is where Mersad lived as well. Mersad that was killed in front of Mola.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And his nickname was the butcher, Mersad?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mersad Mesar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please specify for the record that the witness has shown the last two windows on the first floor as those belonging to the office of the secretary of the local commune and then right next to was the office of the civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the secretary of the local commune had the same glass window on the other side as well, and these glass windows went all the way to the other room where meetings were held, the conference room. So that it was very dangerous to stay here during shelling. All of it was basically just a glass wall, and it wasn't safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the offices of the service for work obligation here in this photograph? Can we see this here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We can. This is the entrance then they used, and these offices did not have the same use they had before the 17th but they were rather assigned to the people who were involved in work obligation. They had their own administration there, their records were kept there, and people usually gathered right here in front of this office here, and as I went into my office, I would normally come from this side because that's where my house was, and I would pass here, I would see these people, I would greet them, and then continue on to my office. So if I happened to pass by on the day when they were there then I would see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please enter into the record that the witness has shown the entrance which is between the white and the green vehicle and is marked with a red arrow as the entrance leading to the office of the work obligation service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Lukic, just go back for one second to page 94 -- page 94, lines 14 to 18, and you asked Mr. Tadic a question what was the role of the Red Cross concerning glazing and funerals, so all of the tasks of civilian protection. Mr. Tadic answered, "No, no, you mean the Red Cross?" You responded with a question, "Yes, the civilian protection." And then you went on about this photographer eve just seen. This all seems a little bit incongruous. The Red Cross or the civilian protection staff, which are we talking about? There doesn't seem to be a real rapport between question and answer here. If you could just clarify that, that would be very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic -- no. I said Red Cross by mistake when mentioning funerals and then Mr. Tadic corrected me saying, "You meant the civilian protection."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let's say a few details regarding that. What was the role of the civilian protection staff when it came to funerals in Samac municipality and what was done regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in Samac, many institutions did not function, especially those which dealt with daily problems. Therefore, all of those services which didn't function were transferred to the civilian protection staff, and this is how it happened that the civilian protection also became a funeral organisation so to speak. In addition to delegating this task to the civilian protection staff, very soon it became clear that coffins also had to be constructed. One couldn't buy them anywhere and to go to Bijeljina which was 80 kilometres away in order to purchase a coffin was ridiculous. Therefore, within the civilian protection staff, a team was organised, a team of people, who built coffins. There was also a need to identify people, not all of the people who had been killed could be identified. Therefore a commission was established called commission for identification. We already had occasion to see here that a large number of civilians were killed by shelling, but a far greater number of soldiers was killed, all of them were buried by civilian protection staff. Not all of them of course but a large number of them, over 450 soldiers were killed in our area, soldiers of the Krajina Brigade, and all of them had to be either buried or sent to their families. Therefore, at the very beginning, we established a morgue which was within the hospital compound near the haemodialysis centre. We needed to supply water, to put up doors and windows there, all of this had been damaged by shelling and then repaired, and it was only after that that a more regular procedure was established to take in the bodies of the dead and to prepare them for burials, in accordance with our customs. First of all, they had to wash and clean the bodies, as much as was possible, in accordance with the customs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's sufficient to say they were responsible for collecting dead bodies and preparing them for burial and burying them. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one small correction in the transcript in page 97, line 25, the witness said, not only soldiers from our area, but soldiers of the Krajina brigade as well. Because this is what I heard that he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned soldiers that were killed, both those who were originally from Samac and those who were from elsewhere but killed in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that about 450 soldiers were killed from Samac area and about 100 or so, several hundred, from Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown document D110/3? And while we are getting the document, [In English] 110/3. D. [Interpretation] The people who worked preparing burials and washing the bodies and so on, was that part of their war obligation or did they receive salaries while they worked with the -- or for the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were involved in the technical matters concerning the burials were all senior citizens, retirees, who did not have a work obligation. They were volunteers. They wanted to contribute something, whereas those people who built coffins, they did that as part of their work obligation. That was assigned to them by the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Tadic, this document has already been admitted into evidence when we spoke to witness called Vukovic. Does this document refer to civilians who were killed in wartime, during war operations? Did you have this document before you and did you analyse it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I know that there was talk that this document has no date. I remember this being mentioned. However, this is an excerpt from the records kept in a certain service, in a certain agency, in the municipality, and these records were kept from the very beginning, and are still kept today, even today if somebody should get killed by stepping on a mine, that remained there from wartime, would be considered a civilian victim of war, and would be entered into these records. So this is just an excerpt, this document is just an excerpt from the records kept by a certain agency. If we take a closer look here, we can see that there are a lot of children, well maybe not a lot of children, but according to my records, there are six children here, over 20 women, and some 20 senior citizens, aged 60 and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can see clearly here that there are people of all ethnicities and that they come both from Samac and from the surrounding villages of the present-day municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the civilian protection staff doing in connection with the list of abandoned shops and what did it do in relation to the list of flats? We have heard testimony about this but can you just briefly describe how this was organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is self-evident. I don't think there is any reason for me to repeat this. There is nothing special I can add. This task was given by the executive board that the list should be drawn up, and it was Mr. Vukovic who worked on these tasks and he described here how this was done. The executive board also set up a commission to make a list of abandoned apartments or flats, and we kept these -- or rather we recorded this and handed it over to the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will now put before you document D63/3.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document D63/3? [In English] 63/3. [Interpretation] What I'm interested in, Mr. Tadic, and you may add whatever you wish, but in the third paragraph, it says, the civilian protection staff was forced to take urgent action to accommodate certain families. What was the reason for this action? Why did these three families have to be accommodated urgently in appropriate temporary accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these three people, Mujo Tokalic, Stefanovic and Cvijeta Djokic, their flats had been so badly damaged by shells that they could not be repaired immediately. Repairs were made only to housing that could be repaired quickly. We didn't undertake any major reconstruction, and these flats were totally destroyed so the people had to be accommodated elsewhere, and if I'm not mistaken it says here somewhere, yes, down here it says, "Please issue approval for these three families and issue a decision on temporary accommodation." The civilian protection staff was asking the executive board to receive these people as such. And there is a place here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in here, I don't know where it is exactly, it says that some people had moved into certain flats unlawfully, illegally, and we were drawing the attention of the executive board to this so that measures could be taken to evict these people. We say, according to our information --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic would you please slow down and speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also wish to inform you that according to our information, people have moved or people or families have moved into some flats of their own accord and then these are listed. So we are informing the executive board of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: When this list was made, and I see that the document is dated the 14th of June, 1992, did you list all such flats regardless of the ethnic affiliation of these flats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer this, let me just say on page 2 it says that two applications handed to us are enclosed with this document for the consideration of the executive board, and as for the flats, we registered all empty flats, whether they were Serb flats, Croatian flats or Muslim flats. There was no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After this recording of flats and shops, did the civilian protection staff have any further role while you were its member on more lists or updating these lists and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian protection staff was given many tasks on a one-time basis. They would carry it out and then it would be taken over by others, and this is what happened here. The services, the professional services, or specialist services were not operating properly at the time, which is why the civilian protection staff was given this task. Later on, these services were established. These services of the executive board. And then they carried on the work. So that we had nothing further to do in this connection. So this part of our task was completed with this letter that was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we will go back to the civilian protection but now I'm interested in something that is very important for these proceedings, and that is the first exchange at Zasavica as we called it. A lot has been said about it before this Court. The Chamber has already learned a lot about it. I would like you to tell us now what you know about this exchange and what your role, if any, was, and whether there is any important information that you feel the Chamber has not heard yet.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot has been said about this exchange, and I was involved in a certain way in these events. After the 8th of May, when the events of the 8th of May took place in Odzak, for a time we -- our relations with Odzak were distant, but then negotiations resumed with the Odzak side and Stjepan Mikic, a colleague of mine by profession, became involved. In view of the fact that we intervened with the International Red Cross, and that there were interventions by others from Belgrade, other associations, the International Red Cross came to Odzak and listed the detainees. I think this was the Red Cross from Osijek because that was its, so to speak, zone of responsibility. After this Stjepan said to me that the Red Cross would also come to Samac. I mean the International Red Cross to list the people in Samac. And this happened. Veljo Maslic spoke of these contacts. I did not have contacts with International Red Cross myself to begin with, in these first contacts. I had contacts with them only later. The other side proposed that we should agree with these representatives of the ICRC that a certain number of these people should be exchanged, especially if they were elderly people or sick people, and they said that the Red Cross would help us with this. I asked what our role in this would be and he said that we would provide the technical conditions that were necessary before the exchange could take place. They already had some experience. This was a little alien to me. I had no experience in these matters and I asked him where this could be done. He responded that this would best be done in the Zasavica area and the Balegovac and Donja Dubica area, and that this should be done through Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "he," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Stjepan Mikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to avoid confusion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where did you talk?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we talked through the communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was at that time to get a cease-fire to take place and then later on there was talk of getting a boat. He told me that he was unable to get a boat and that we should try to get one and we did. And then we had to find the transport, because there are some six or seven kilometres between Samac and the area where we agreed that the exchange should take place. Of course, there were no technical obstacles because all this could very easily be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you meet the representatives of the ICRC for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met them for the first time when the list of detainees was drawn up, the list of detainees to be exchanged. They invited me to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are representatives of the International Red Cross invited me to the school where they were conducting a -- where they were drawing up a list of these people. They were in the corridor, and I arrived there. There was a man there and an interpreter. At that point, the girl mentioned here, Catharine, wasn't present. I met her later. This man asked me through the interpreter when the transportation would be provided, and whether everything was all right. I said that it was, that we had found a boat, that we had secured a cease-fire, and that the vehicles would be ready whenever he said they were needed. He said they should come to the school around noon. I left, and I sent the vehicles along. These were the same vehicles taking soldiers to take up their shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This conversation with the representatives of the International Red Cross, just for the sake of clarification, was conducted on the same day that the exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day when these vehicles were to be provided. Of course, I had contacted, I think it was the first detachment that was responsible for that area in Crkvina, and told them about this, and they said there would be no problems, that there were no major operations going on at that moment, but that they would make sure that the soldiers would not be near the place where the exchange was to occur. And that's what happened. They did what they were supposed to do and the vehicles went to the school and collected these people and brought them to the place agreed upon for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bank of the River Bosna, did anything happen? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that spot, next to me, there were quite a few people who either officially or unofficially, were there, but many of them were simply people who had come there out of curiosity and the police had to keep them away because it was dangerous for such large numbers of people to be present. That's why the police tried to keep order and got the people to stand about a kilometre away from the area: The representative of the International Red Cross was there and there was a man who knew how to operate the boat, and then what happened was what Veljo described, they went there but as for the method, people were -- people's names were called out from the list, they would approach the desk that had been set up there, and they would tell the man there whether they wished to cross over to the other side or not. Those who wished to cross over boarded the boat. Those who didn't want to remained standing by the desk. I think that five or six people got into the boat. They would come up to the desk. So they went to the boat in groups of five or six. And that's how it went on until ten people were left lined who did not want to cross over. He asked them again, are you sure you don't want to go? And they said they didn't want to go. But on the other side, there were also ten people who didn't cross over. I asked him why haven't these people come here? And he said they would have to let them go but maybe they didn't want to go. There was no way we could check this so that's where the matter ended. People were -- I mean the Serbs who had crossed over and the Croats who had stayed behind were put on to trucks and taken to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have before me the original of document D69/3 ter ID. There is a copy in the file which has been given only an identification number, so I now ask that the original document be put before the witness so that the witness can give us his comment as to authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you familiar with this document? Do you know about it personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And what it says up here, exchanged, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next to some names, there is a remark. Do you know that where it says "refused" next to a name that these are people who stayed behind, that did not cross over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to every name, there is a tick, and that's for our records, indicating that they crossed over, but those who refused to go over, for example, next to number 24, Ivo Petric, and then 39, Tadija Pejic and so on, these are the people who didn't want to cross over to the opposite side. Under number 3, she is a witness of ours, or he, Osman Jasarevic, who spoke of a list or rather of a list being made in the school, and there is another Muslim here who did cross over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you see number 49, Andrija Petric, he is still in Samac. He came back on that occasion, and he's in Samac still. I can't remember all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter but if the Prosecution has no further objections, I now ask that this document be given a number as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objections, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that this be adduced into evidence because it's a much better copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D69/3 and D69/3 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the exchange and the completion thereof, did representatives of the ICRC had any objections to your work or how the civilian protection staff handled the matter? Do you know anything about the International Red Cross's opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this exchange in this restaurant in Tekstilac mentioned earlier, a dinner was prepared for all the exchanged persons, including the representatives of the International Red Cross and the few of us who took part in the whole affair. I thanked them for their great efforts because they really made tremendous efforts, especially this woman who crossed across -- who went over the River Bosna. She was all covered in mud and really had terrible efforts, and then I learned from them that those people who refused to cross over or to be exchanged, that as of that moment, they were free citizens, they were free to go home or any place they wished. That was a significant revelation because it was particularly this principle that we applied in our work from then on. She also wanted to know if those people went home, I replied, yes they did. And then she explained to me that that was the principle employed or -- and required by the International Red Cross to be practised. They had no objections whatsoever, either to our organising means of transportation and the method of work of our local Red Cross organisation. Since my house is in close proximity of the Tekstilac, we later on went to my house, sat in the garden, had a coffee, ate pancakes, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously, one of the effects of this exchange was that you learned how the principles of the International Red Cross worked in practice. Was there any other aspect of this exchange that helped you acquire some new knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From those people who came, and you can see there were lots of relatives of mine and I knew virtually all of them, most of them came to my house later. We sat there and talked there. They described to me the situation prevailing on the other side, meaning in Odzak, and they spoke about some individuals that should have been given -- that should be given priority in exchange because of their condition. Later, I heard from the ten people that were returned, I remember but I didn't show it, so one of the ten people who were returned, a friend of mine by the name of Muskic told me that the significant thing was that he returned, because the making of the list in Odzak went in more or less this order: First, the ICRC representatives from Odzak would come with a piece of paper and a pencil and then they will say who wants to be exchanged. But of those who are over 65 years of age or who are underage should be included in the list. People wanted to know where the exchange was going to take place and they replied that it would take place in Balegovac. That arose some unpleasant memories in people's minds from the Second World War and they felt reluctant to enter their names in this list. It took quite a long time for the list to be made at all. The first people who were entered into the list were those who didn't have any association with these unpleasant events, and finally, my uncle was put on the list and I said -- and he said if that was my destiny I would put my name on the list. The significant thing is that this man who returned to Odzak told the other people that the exchange was completed, that it was done, and that people were not killed, as had originally been thought. So that was of great significance for all future exchanges and for the work of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we wrap up for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Court will adjourn and continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
